metadata.title: Spectral inequalities for nonnegative tensors and their tropical analogues

extraction_notes.note: Numbered equation (7.2) retyped as a claim: the text derives it ('Combine the above theorem with (4.1) to give a stronger version of (3.20)') and it has its own prose proof; could also stay an equation.

Theorem 3 is introduced as a summary of known results (CPZ08, FGH), so it is external although the paper writes its own proof; that proof is paper and is separated from the theorem by a sentence, so its proves edge was added by hand.
Example 1 contains a table of all nine 3-cycles for n=2, d=4 with their weights; kept inside the example statement, no separate nodes.
The proof of Theorem 31 is organized by run-in labels \emph{1}. ... \emph{8}. that the parser did not report as labels; one step per part was emitted anyway.
Introduction motivation, the comparisons with ZQL10/Fri81/TFL11 and the discussion of amoebas and tropical roots after Corollary 25 are discursive and were not made nodes.

nodes.name: Ground field F
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbb{F}$ be either the field of complex numbers $\mathbb{C}$ or of real numbers $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions of irreducibility

nodes.name: Tensor index notation m, m^{x d}, [d], F^m
nodes.statement: Denote \begin{eqnarray} &&\mathbf{m}:=(m_1,\ldots,m_d),\quad m^{\times d}:=(\underbrace{m,\ldots,m}_{d\;\text{times}}), \qquad [d]:=\{1,\dots,d\}\\ &&\mathbb{F}^{\mathbf{m}}:=\otimes_{i\in[d]} \mathbb{F}^{m_i}=\mathbb{F}^{m_1\times\ldots\times m_d}, \qquad \mathbb{F}^{m^{\times d}}:= \otimes^d \mathbb{F}^m=\mathbb{F}^{m\times \ldots\times m},\notag \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Notation for tensor dimensions, index sets [d], and the tensor spaces F^m and F^{m^{x d}}.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions of irreducibility

nodes.name: Tensor index notation (2.1)
nodes.statement: &&\mathbf{m}:=(m_1,\ldots,m_d),\quad m^{\times d}:=(\underbrace{m,\ldots,m}_{d\;\text{times}}), \qquad [d]:=\{1,\dots,d\}\\ &&\mathbb{F}^{\mathbf{m}}:=\otimes_{i\in[d]} \mathbb{F}^{m_i}=\mathbb{F}^{m_1\times\ldots\times m_d}, \qquad \mathbb{F}^{m^{\times d}}:= \otimes^d \mathbb{F}^m=\mathbb{F}^{m\times \ldots\times m},\notag
nodes.section: 2 Definitions of irreducibility
nodes.label: defbm

nodes.name: Equidimensional tensors
nodes.statement: The vector space $\mathbb{F}^{m^{\times d}}$ is called the space of \emph{equidimensional} tensors.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions of irreducibility

nodes.name: Nonnegative reals R_+
nodes.statement: We shall denote by $\mathbb{R}_+$ the set of nonnegative numbers.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions of irreducibility

nodes.name: Cone of nonnegative tensors
nodes.statement: Then, $\mathbb{R}_+^{\mathbf{m}}\subset \mathbb{R}^{\mathbf{m}}$ is the cone of {\em nonnegative tensors}.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions of irreducibility

nodes.name: Undirected d-partite graph G(F) of a tensor
nodes.statement: Assume that $\mathcal{F}\in \mathbb{R}_+^{\mathbf{m}}$. We associate with $\mathcal{F}$ an {\em undirected} $d$-partite graph $G(\mathcal{F})=(V,E(\mathcal{F}))$, the vertex set of which is the disjoint union $V=\cup_{j=1}^d V_j$, with $V_j=[m_j], j\in [d]$. The edge $(i_k,i_l)\in V_k\times V_l, k\ne l$ belongs to $E(\mathcal{F})$ if and only if $f_{i_1,i_2,\ldots,i_d}>0$ for some $d-2$ indices $\{i_1,\ldots,i_d\}\backslash\{i_k,i_l\}$.
nodes.statement_short: The d-partite graph on index sets, with an edge between indices of different modes when some entry containing both is positive.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions of irreducibility

nodes.name: Weakly indecomposable tensor
nodes.statement: The tensor $\mathcal{F}$ is called \emph{weakly indecomposable} if the graph $G(\mathcal{F})$ is connected.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions of irreducibility

nodes.name: Indecomposable tensor
nodes.statement: We call $\mathcal{F}$ \emph{indecomposable} if for each proper nonempty subset $\emptyset \ne I\subsetneqq V$, the following condition holds: Assume that $I$ does not contain $V_p\cup V_q$ for any $p\ne q \in [d]$. Let $J:=V\backslash I$. Then there exists $k\in [d]$, $i_k\in I\cap V_k$ and $i_j\in J\cap V_j$ for each $j\in [d] \backslash\{k\}$ such that $f_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}>0$.
nodes.statement_short: F is indecomposable if every proper index subset I not containing two whole modes admits a positive entry with one index in I and the rest outside.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions of irreducibility

nodes.name: Indecomposable implies weakly indecomposable (FGH)
nodes.statement: It is shown in \cite{FGH} that if $\mathcal{F}$ is indecomposable then $\mathcal{F}$ is weakly indecomposable.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions of irreducibility

nodes.name: Directed graph of an equidimensional tensor
nodes.statement: Assume that $\mathcal{F}$ is an equidimensional tensor in $\mathbb{R}_+^{m^{\times d}}$. With $\mathcal{F}$ we associate a directed graph $\vec{G}(\mathcal{F})=(V, E(\mathcal{F}))$, where $V=[m]$. The diedge from $i$ to $j$ belongs to $E(\mathcal{F})$ if and only if $f_{i,j_1,\ldots,j_{d-1}}>0$ for some $d-1$ indices $\{j_1,\ldots,j_{d-1}\}$ such that $j=j_k$ for some $k\in[d-1]$.
nodes.statement_short: Digraph on [n] with an arc i->j when some positive entry f_{i,j_1..j_{d-1}} has j among the last indices.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions of irreducibility

nodes.name: Weakly irreducible tensor
nodes.statement: We say that $\mathcal{F}$ is {\em weakly irreducible} if $\vec{G}(\mathcal{F})$ is strongly connected.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions of irreducibility

nodes.name: Irreducible tensor
nodes.statement: We call $\mathcal{F}$ \emph{irreducible} if for each proper nonempty subset $\emptyset \ne I\subsetneqq V$, there exist $i\in I$ and $j_1,\ldots,j_{d-1}\in V\setminus I$ such that $f_{i,j_2,\ldots,j_{d-1}}>0$.
nodes.statement_short: F is irreducible if every proper nonempty index subset I has an entry f_{i,j...}>0 with i in I and the other indices outside I.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions of irreducibility

nodes.name: Indecomposability and irreducibility imply their weak forms
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}\in \mathbb{R}_+^{\mathbf{m}}$. Then \begin{enumerate} \item If $\mathcal{F}$ is indecomposable then $\mathcal{F}$ is weakly indecomposable. \item Assume that $m_1=\ldots=m_d=m$. If $\mathcal{F}$ is irreducible then $\mathcal{F}$ is weakly irreducible. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Indecomposable tensors are weakly indecomposable; irreducible equidimensional tensors are weakly irreducible.
nodes.section: 2 Definitions of irreducibility
nodes.label: strngimpweak

nodes.name: Tensor product of tensors
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{m}=(m_1,\ldots,m_d), \mathbf{n}=(n_1,\ldots,n_e)$. Assume that $\mathcal{F}=[f_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]\in\mathbb{F}^{\mathbf{m}},\mathcal{G}=[g_{j_1,\ldots,j_e}]\in \mathbb{F}^{\mathbf{n}}$ are given. Then the entries of the tensor product $\mathcal{F}\otimes\mathcal{G}\in\mathbb{F}^{(\mathbf{m},\mathbf{n})}:=\mathbb{F}^{\mathbf{m}}\otimes \mathbb{F}^{\mathbf{n}}$ are given by $ [f_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}g_{j_1,\ldots,j_e}]$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Standard facts on tensors

nodes.name: Subtensor
nodes.statement: Assume that $d=e$. Then $\mathcal{G}$ is called a subtensor of $\mathcal{F}$ if the following conditions hold. First, $n_k\leqslant m_k$ for $k\in [d]$. Second, for each $k\in[d]$ there exists a sequence $1\leqslant i_{1,k}<\ldots<i_{n_k,k}\leqslant m_k$ such that $g_{j_1,\ldots,j_d}=f_{i_{j_1,1},\ldots,i_{j_d,d}}$.
nodes.statement_short: G is a subtensor of F if it is obtained by selecting increasing index subsequences in every mode.
nodes.section: 3.1 Standard facts on tensors

nodes.name: Product dimension vector m o n
nodes.statement: Define $\mathbf{m}\circ\mathbf{n}:=(m_1n_1,\ldots,m_dn_d)$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Standard facts on tensors

nodes.name: Isomorphism of tensor product space and Kronecker space
nodes.statement: Then $\mathbb{F}^{(\mathbf{m},\mathbf{n})}$ and $\mathbb{F}^{\mathbf{m}\circ\mathbf{n}}$ are isomorphic as vector spaces. Furthermore, the isomorphism $\iota:\mathbb{F}^{(\mathbf{m},\mathbf{n})}\to\mathbb{F}^{\mathbf{m}\circ\mathbf{n}}$ maps rank one tensors to rank one tensors, but $\iota^{-1}$ does not preserves the rank one tensors.
nodes.section: 3.1 Standard facts on tensors
conclusions: $\mathbb{F}^{(\mathbf{m},\mathbf{n})}$ and $\mathbb{F}^{\mathbf{m}\circ\mathbf{n}}$ are isomorphic as vector spaces

nodes.name: Kronecker product of tensors
nodes.statement: We define the Kronecker product of tensors $\mathcal{F}\otimes_{\mathop{\mathrm{Kr}}\nolimits}\mathcal{G}=[h_{(i_1,j_1),\ldots,(i_d,j_d)}]\in \mathbb{F}^{\mathbf{m}\circ\mathbf{n}}$, where $h_{(i_1,j_1),\ldots,(i_d,j_d)}=f_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}g_{j_1,\ldots,j_d}$, which extends the classical definition of the Kronecker product of matrices.
nodes.section: 3.1 Standard facts on tensors

nodes.name: Sub-dimension vector m(J)
nodes.statement: Let $J=\{1\leqslant j_1<\ldots<j_k\leqslant d\}$ be a nonempty subset of $[d]$. Denote $\mathbf{m}(J)=(m_{j_1},\ldots,m_{j_k})$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Standard facts on tensors

nodes.name: Contraction T x S of tensors
nodes.statement: Assume that $\mathcal{T}=[t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]\in\mathbb{F}^{\mathbf{m}},\mathcal{S}=[s_{i_{j_1},\ldots,i_{j_k}}]\in\mathbb{F}^{\mathbf{m}(J)}$. Then $\mathcal{T}\times \mathcal{S}=\mathcal{S}\times \mathcal{T}=\mathbb{F}^{\mathbf{m}([d]\setminus J)}$ is a $d-k$ tensor obtained by the contraction on the indices in $J$. That is, the entries of $\mathcal{T}\times \mathcal{S}$ are \[\sum_{i_{j_1}\in [m_{j_1}],\ldots, i_{j_k}\in[m_{j_k}]} t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d} s_{i_{j_1} ,\ldots,i_{j_k}}.\]
nodes.statement_short: T x S is the (d-k)-tensor obtained by contracting T with S on the indices in J.
nodes.section: 3.1 Standard facts on tensors

nodes.name: Hadamard product of tensors
nodes.statement: Furthermore, we define the Hadamard product $\mathcal{T}\circ \mathcal{S}=\mathcal{S}\circ\mathcal{T}:=[t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d} s_{i_{j_1},\ldots,i_{j_k}}]\in \mathbb{F}^{\mathbf{m}}$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Standard facts on tensors

nodes.name: Hadamard product is a subtensor of the Kronecker product
nodes.statement: Assume that $J=[d]$, i.e.\ $\mathbf{m}=\mathbf{n}$. Then $\mathcal{T}\circ \mathcal{S}\in\mathbb{F}^{\mathbf{m}}$ can be viewed as a \emph{subtensor} of $\mathcal{T}\otimes_{\mathop{\mathrm{Kr}}\nolimits}\mathcal{S}$ where we choose $i_1=j_1\in [m_1],\ldots,i_d=j_d\in [m_d]$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Standard facts on tensors
conclusions: $\mathcal{T}\circ \mathcal{S}\in\mathbb{F}^{\mathbf{m}}$ can be viewed as a \emph{subtensor} of $\mathcal{T}\otimes_{\mathop{\mathrm{Kr}}\nolimits}\mathcal{S}$

nodes.name: Inner product of tensors
nodes.statement: In fact, $\an{\mathcal{T},\mathcal{S}}:=\mathcal{T}\times \mathcal{S}$ is an inner product on $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbf{m}}$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Standard facts on tensors

nodes.name: Hilbert-Schmidt norm
nodes.statement: The Hilbert-Schmidt norm on $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbf{m}}$ is defined by $\|\mathcal{T}\|:=\sqrt{\an{\mathcal{T},\mathcal{T}}}$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Standard facts on tensors

nodes.name: Tensor product of vectors over J
nodes.statement: For $\mathbf{x}_j\in \mathbb{F}^{m_j}, j\in J$, we denote $\otimes_{j\in J} \mathbf{x}_j:=\mathbf{x}_{j_1}\otimes\dots\otimes \mathbf{x}_{j_k}\in \mathbb{F}^{\mathbf{m}(J)}$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Standard facts on tensors

nodes.name: Tensor power and Hadamard power of a vector
nodes.statement: Furthermore for $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_m)^\top\in \mathbb{F}^m$ and for any positive integer $k$ we denote $\otimes^k {\mathbf{x}}:=\underbrace{{\mathbf{x}}\otimes\dots\otimes{\mathbf{x}}}_{k\;\text{times}}\in \mathbb{F}^{m^{\times k}}, \mathbf{x}^{\circ k}:=(x_1^k,\ldots,x_m^k)^\top\in \mathbb{F}^m$.
nodes.section: 3.1 Standard facts on tensors

nodes.name: Symmetric tensor
nodes.statement: A tensor $\mathcal{S}=[s_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]\in\mathbb{F}^{n^{\times d}}$ is called symmetric if $s_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}= s_{i_{\omega(1)},\ldots,i_{\omega(d)}}$ for every permutation $\omega:[d]\to[d]$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Symmetric tensors

nodes.name: Space of symmetric tensors S^d F^n
nodes.statement: Denote by $\mathrm{S}^d\mathbb{F}^n\subset \otimes^d\mathbb{F}^{n^{\times d}}$ the vector space of $d$-mode symmetric tensors on $\mathbb{F}^n$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Symmetric tensors

nodes.name: Homogeneous polynomial of a symmetric tensor
nodes.statement: A tensor $\mathcal{S}\in\mathrm{S}^d\mathbb{F}^n$ defines a unique homogeneous polynomial of degree $d$ in $n$ variables $f(\mathbf{x})=\mathcal{S}\times\otimes^d\mathbf{x}$, where \begin{eqnarray*} f(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{ j_k+1\in [d+1],k\in[n], j_1+\cdots +j_n=d} \frac{d!}{j_1!\cdots j_n!} f_{j_1,\ldots,j_n} x_1^{j_1}\cdots x_n^{j_n}. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.section: 3.2 Symmetric tensors

nodes.name: Polynomial expansion of a symmetric tensor
nodes.statement: f(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{ j_k+1\in [d+1],k\in[n], j_1+\cdots +j_n=d} \frac{d!}{j_1!\cdots j_n!} f_{j_1,\ldots,j_n} x_1^{j_1}\cdots x_n^{j_n}.
nodes.section: 3.2 Symmetric tensors
nodes.label: defpolfx

nodes.name: Index set J(d,n)
nodes.statement: Denote by $J(d,n)$ be the set of all $\mathbf{j}=(j_1,\ldots,j_n)\in\mathbf{Z}_+^n$ appearing in the above definition of $f(\mathbf{x})$: \begin{eqnarray*} J(d,n)= \{\mathbf{j}=(j_1,\ldots,j_n)\in\mathbf{Z}_+^n,\; j_1+\cdots+j_n=d\}. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.section: 3.2 Symmetric tensors

nodes.name: Definition of J(d,n)
nodes.statement: J(d,n)= \{\mathbf{j}=(j_1,\ldots,j_n)\in\mathbf{Z}_+^n,\; j_1+\cdots+j_n=d\}.
nodes.section: 3.2 Symmetric tensors
nodes.label: defJdn

nodes.name: Cardinality of J(d,n)
nodes.statement: It is well known that $|J(d,n)|={n+d-1\choose n}={n+d-1\choose d-1}$ \cite{FW16}.
nodes.section: 3.2 Symmetric tensors

nodes.name: Multinomial coefficient c(j)
nodes.statement: Define $c(\mathbf{j})=\frac{d!}{j_1!\cdots j_n!}$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Symmetric tensors

nodes.name: Monomial x^j
nodes.statement: For $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)^\top\in\mathbb{F}^n$ and $\mathbf{j}=(j_1,\ldots,j_n)\in J(d,n)$ let $\mathbf{x}^{\mathbf{j}}$ be the monomial $x_1^{j_1}\cdots x_n^{j_n}$.
nodes.section: 3.2 Symmetric tensors

nodes.name: Space of homogeneous polynomials P(d,n,F)
nodes.statement: Thus $\mathrm{S}^d\mathbb{F}^n$ is isomorphic to $\mathrm{P}(d,n,\mathbb{F})$, the space of homogeneous polynomials of degree $d$ in $n$ variables.
nodes.section: 3.2 Symmetric tensors

nodes.name: Gradient formula for symmetric tensors
nodes.statement: Assume that $\mathcal{S}\in\mathrm{S}^d\mathbb{F}^n$ and let $f(\mathbf{x})=\mathcal{S}\times\otimes^d\mathbf{x}$. Then \cite{FW16}: \[\mathcal{S}\times(\otimes^{d-1}\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{d}\nabla f(\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{d}(\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}(\mathbf{x}),\ldots,\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_n}(\mathbf{x})).\]
nodes.statement_short: Contracting a symmetric tensor with d-1 copies of x gives (1/d) times the gradient of its polynomial.
nodes.section: 3.2 Symmetric tensors

nodes.name: Homogeneous map of a tensor
nodes.statement: With an equidimensional tensor $\mathcal{F}\in \mathbb{C}^{n^{\times d}}$ we associate a homogeneous map of degree $d-1$ given as $\mathbf{x}\mapsto\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{x})=\mathcal{F}\times \otimes^{d-1}\mathbf{x}$, where the contraction is \emph{on the last} $d-1$ indices of $\mathcal{F}$.
nodes.section: 3.3 The homogeneous eigenvalue problem

nodes.name: Subspace of partially symmetric tensors
nodes.statement: For $\mathbb{F}\in\{\mathbb{C},\mathbb{R}\}$ we denote by $\mathbb{F}^{n^{\times d}}_{ps}$ the subspace of tensors whose entries $t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}$ are symmetric with respect to the indices $i_2,\ldots,i_d$.
nodes.section: 3.3 The homogeneous eigenvalue problem

nodes.name: Partially symmetric tensor
nodes.statement: We call such tensors \emph{partially symmetric}.
nodes.section: 3.3 The homogeneous eigenvalue problem

nodes.name: Cone of nonnegative partially symmetric tensors
nodes.statement: Denote by $\mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}\subset \mathbb{R}_{ps}^{n^{\times d}}$ the cone of nonnegative partially symmetric tensors.
nodes.section: 3.3 The homogeneous eigenvalue problem

nodes.name: Polynomial map F of a partially symmetric tensor
nodes.statement: We observe that a partially symmetric tensor $\mathcal{F}\in\mathbb{F}^{n^{\times d}}_{ps}$ is in one-to-one correspondence with a polynomial map $\mathbf{F}=(F_1,\ldots,F_n):\mathbb{F}^n\to\mathbb{F}^n$, where each $F_i(\mathbf{x})=(\mathcal{F}\otimes (\otimes^{d-1}\mathbf{x}))_i$ is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $d-1$ in $\mathbf{x}$.
nodes.section: 3.3 The homogeneous eigenvalue problem

nodes.name: Digraph arcs via partial derivatives
nodes.statement: Assume that $\mathcal{F}\in\mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$. Then the digraph $\vec{G}(\mathcal{F})$ contains a diedge $(i,j)$ if and only if $\frac{\partial F_i(\mathbf{x})}{\partial x_j}> 0$ for $\mathbf{x}>\mathbf{0}$.
nodes.section: 3.3 The homogeneous eigenvalue problem
conclusions: the digraph $\vec{G}(\mathcal{F})$ contains a diedge $(i,j)$ if and only if $\frac{\partial F_i(\mathbf{x})}{\partial x_j}> 0$ for $\mathbf{x}>\mathbf{0}$

nodes.name: Homogeneous eigenvalue problem
nodes.statement: The homogeneous eigenvalue problem considered in this paper is \begin{equation} \mathcal{F}\times \otimes^{d-1}\mathbf{x}=\lambda\mathbf{x}^{\circ (d-1)}, \quad \mathbf{x}\ne \mathbf{0}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Find lambda and nonzero x with F x^{d-1} = lambda x^{[d-1]}.
nodes.section: 3.3 The homogeneous eigenvalue problem

nodes.name: Homogeneous eigenvalue problem (3.1)
nodes.statement: \mathcal{F}\times \otimes^{d-1}\mathbf{x}=\lambda\mathbf{x}^{\circ (d-1)}, \quad \mathbf{x}\ne \mathbf{0}.
nodes.section: 3.3 The homogeneous eigenvalue problem
nodes.label: homeigprob

nodes.name: Pencil eigenvalue problem
nodes.statement: As for matrices, for $\mathcal{F},\mathcal{S}\in \mathbb{C}^{n^{\times d}}_{ps}$ we can consider the pencil eigenvalue problem \begin{equation} \mathcal{F}\times \otimes^{d-1} \mathbf{x}=\lambda \mathcal{S}\times \otimes^{d-1} \mathbf{x}, \quad \mathbf{x}\ne \mathbf{0}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.3 The homogeneous eigenvalue problem

nodes.name: Pencil eigenvalue problem (3.2)
nodes.statement: \mathcal{F}\times \otimes^{d-1} \mathbf{x}=\lambda \mathcal{S}\times \otimes^{d-1} \mathbf{x}, \quad \mathbf{x}\ne \mathbf{0}.
nodes.section: 3.3 The homogeneous eigenvalue problem
nodes.label: homepeneigprob

nodes.name: Diagonal identity tensor I_{n,d}
nodes.statement: For $\mathcal{S}=\mathcal{I}_{n,d}$, where $\mathcal{I}_{n,d}$ is the diagonal tensor $[\delta_{i_1i_2}\ldots\delta_{i_1i_d}]\in \mathbb{C}^{n^{\times d}}_{ps}$, the system \eqref{homepeneigprob} reduces to \eqref{homeigprob}.
nodes.section: 3.3 The homogeneous eigenvalue problem

nodes.name: Shorthand I
nodes.statement: When no ambiguity arises we denote $\mathcal{I}_{n,d}$ by $\mathcal{I}$.
nodes.section: 3.3 The homogeneous eigenvalue problem

nodes.name: Singular tensor
nodes.statement: The tensor $\mathcal{S}$ is called \emph{singular} if the system \begin{equation} \mathcal{S}\times\otimes^{d-1}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0} \end{equation} has a nontrivial solution.
nodes.section: 3.3 The homogeneous eigenvalue problem

nodes.name: Singular system (3.3)
nodes.statement: \mathcal{S}\times\otimes^{d-1}\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{0}
nodes.section: 3.3 The homogeneous eigenvalue problem

nodes.name: Nonsingular tensor
nodes.statement: Otherwise $\mathcal{S}$ is called nonsingular.
nodes.section: 3.3 The homogeneous eigenvalue problem

nodes.name: Resultant of a homogeneous system
nodes.statement: There exists an irreducible polynomial $\mathrm{res\;} :\mathbb{C}^{n^{\times d}}_{ps}\to \mathbb{C}$ with the following properties \cite[Chapter 13]{GKZ}. First, $\mathcal{S}$ is singular if and only if $\mathrm{res\;} \mathcal{S}=0$. Second for a general singular $\mathcal{S}$ the set of all nontrivial solutions is a line, i.e., a one dimensional vector space. Third, the degree of $\mathrm{res\;} $ is $n (d-1)^{n-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: The resultant is an irreducible polynomial vanishing exactly on singular tensors, of degree n(d-1)^{n-1}.

conclusions: $\mathcal{S}$ is singular if and only if $\mathrm{res\;} \mathcal{S}=0$

nodes.name: Characteristic equation of a pencil
nodes.statement: Hence, to find all eigenvectors of the system \eqref{homepeneigprob}, one first finds all the solutions of the \emph{characteristic equation} \begin{equation} \mathrm{res\;}(\lambda\mathcal{S}-\mathcal{F})=(\mathrm{res\;} \mathcal{S})\lambda^{n(d-1)^{n-1}}+\sum_{j\in [n(d-1)^{n-1}]} c_j(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{F})\lambda^{n(d-1)^{n-1}-j}. \end{equation} Here $c_j(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{F})$ is a homogeneous polynomial of total degree $n(d-1)^{n-1}$ and the partial degrees in the $\mathcal{S}$ and $\mathcal{F}$ variables are $n(d-1)^{n-1}-j$ and $j$ respectively.
nodes.section: 3.3 The homogeneous eigenvalue problem

nodes.name: Characteristic equation (3.4)
nodes.statement: \mathrm{res\;}(\lambda\mathcal{S}-\mathcal{F})=(\mathrm{res\;} \mathcal{S})\lambda^{n(d-1)^{n-1}}+\sum_{j\in [n(d-1)^{n-1}]} c_j(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{F})\lambda^{n(d-1)^{n-1}-j}.

nodes.name: Eigenvalues of a pencil
nodes.statement: After finding all the solutions of \eqref{chareqpen}, called the {\em eigenvalues} of the pencil $(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{S})$, one needs to find the corresponding eigenvectors.
nodes.section: 3.3 The homogeneous eigenvalue problem

nodes.name: Number of pencil eigenvalues
nodes.statement: If $\mathcal{S}$ is nonsingular then the pencil $(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{S})$ has exactly $n(d-1)^{n-1}$ eigenvalues counting with multiplicities.
nodes.section: 3.3 The homogeneous eigenvalue problem
conclusions: the pencil $(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{S})$ has exactly $n(d-1)^{n-1}$ eigenvalues counting with multiplicities

nodes.name: Generic tensors have simple eigenvalues
nodes.statement: Then a general $\mathcal{F}$ has $n(d-1)^{n-1}$ distinct eigenvalues, and to each eigenvalue $\lambda_i$ corresponds a unique eigenvector $\mathbf{x}_i\ne \mathbf{0}$, up to a nonzero factor. (I.e., the eigenspace is the line in $\mathbb{C}^n$ spanned by $\mathbf{x}_i$.)

conclusions: has $n(d-1)^{n-1}$ distinct eigenvalues, and to each eigenvalue $\lambda_i$ corresponds a unique eigenvector $\mathbf{x}_i\ne \mathbf{0}$, up to a nonzero factor

nodes.name: Spectral radius of a tensor

nodes.statement: \rho(\mathcal{F}):=\max\{|\lambda_i(\mathcal{F})|, \;i\in [n(d-1)^{n-1}]\}

nodes.name: Proof of continuity of the spectral radius
nodes.statement: Since the roots of a polynomial depend continuously of its coefficients, using the characteristic equation \eqref{chareqpen}, we arrive at the following result.

nodes.name: Continuity of the spectral radius

assumptions: Let $\rho(\mathcal{F})$ be the spectral radius for the eigenvalue problem \eqref{homeigprob} given by \eqref{defspecradF}.

nodes.statement: For matrices, i.e.\ when $d=2$, the equality holds.

nodes.name: Proof of equality for matrices
nodes.statement: This follows from the fact that the number of eigenvalues of $\mathcal{E}\otimes_{\mathop{\mathrm{Kr}}\nolimits}\mathcal{F}$ of the form $\mu\lambda$ is exactly $mn$, which is the total number of the eigenvalues of the matrix $\mathcal{E}\otimes_{\mathop{\mathrm{Kr}}\nolimits}\mathcal{F}$.
nodes.statement_short: Count: the products mu*lambda already exhaust all mn eigenvalues of the Kronecker product.
nodes.section: 3.3 The homogeneous eigenvalue problem

nodes.name: Equality unclear for d>2
nodes.statement: For $d>2$ the number of eigenvalues of the form $\mu\lambda$ is $(m(d-1)^{m-1})(n(d-1)^{n-1})$ which is strictly less than $(mn)(d-1)^{(mn)-1}$, the number of the eigenvalues of $\mathcal{E}\otimes_{\mathop{\mathrm{Kr}}\nolimits}\mathcal{F}$, for $m,n>1$. So it is not clear that the equality in \eqref{EFKronspecradin} always holds for $d>2$.
nodes.statement_short: For d>2 the product eigenvalues do not exhaust the spectrum, so equality in (3.8) is not clear in general.

nodes.name: Perron-Frobenius theorem for nonnegative tensors
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{T}\in\mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$. Then $\rho(\mathcal{T})$ is an eigenvalue of $\mathcal{T}$ corresponding to a nonnegative eigenvector \begin{equation} \mathcal{T}(\mathbf{v})=\rho(\mathcal{T})\mathbf{v}^{\circ(d-1)}, \quad \mathbf{v} \gneq \mathbf{0}. \end{equation} Furthermore \begin{equation} \rho(\mathcal{T})=\inf_{\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)^\top>\mathbf{0}} \max_{i\in [n]}\frac{\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x})_i}{x_i^{d-1}}. \end{equation} Assume that $\mathcal{T}$ is irreducible. Then $\mathcal{T}$ has a nonnegative eigenvector $\mathbf{u}$, which is positive, and unique (up to a scalar multiple). The corresponding eigenvalue is the spectral radius $\rho(\mathcal{T})$ \begin{equation} \mathcal{T}(\mathbf{u})=\rho(\mathcal{T})\mathbf{u}^{\circ(d-1)}, \quad \mathbf{u}>\mathbf{0}. \end{equation} Furthermore $\rho(\mathcal{T})$ has the characterizations \begin{equation} \rho(\mathcal{T})=\min_{\mathbf{x}>\mathbf{0}} \max_{i\in [n]}\frac{\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x})_i}{x_i^{d-1}}=\max_{\mathbf{x}>\mathbf{0}} \min_{i\in [n]}\frac{\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x})_i}{x_i^{d-1}}. \end{equation} Assume that $\mathcal{T}$ is weakly irreducible. Then $\mathcal{T}$ has a unique positive eigenvector $\mathbf{u}$, which satisfies \eqref{poseigvec}. Furthermore \begin{equation} \rho(\mathcal{T})=\min_{\mathbf{x}>\mathbf{0}} \max_{i\in [n]}\frac{\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x})_i}{x_i^{d-1}}=\max_{\mathbf{x}\gneq\mathbf{0}} \min_{i\in [n], x_i>0}\frac{\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x})_i}{x_i^{d-1}}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: rho(T) is an eigenvalue with nonnegative eigenvector and Collatz-Wielandt formulas; positive unique eigenvector under (weak) irreducibility.
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Collatz-Wielandt min-max for irreducible tensors (3.12)
nodes.statement: \rho(\mathcal{T})=\min_{\mathbf{x}>\mathbf{0}} \max_{i\in [n]}\frac{\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x})_i}{x_i^{d-1}}=\max_{\mathbf{x}>\mathbf{0}} \min_{i\in [n]}\frac{\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x})_i}{x_i^{d-1}}.
