nodes.label: minmaxrhowirchar

nodes.name: Proof of the Perron-Frobenius theorem for tensors
nodes.statement: Suppose first that $\mathcal{T}$ is irreducible. Then the results in \cite{CPZ08} show that any nonnegative eigenvector is positive, and that this eigenvector is unique up to a scalar factor. It corresponds to a positive eigenvalue which is the spectral radius of $\mathcal{T}$. Furthermore, the characterization in \eqref{minmaxrhoirchar} holds. Assume that $\mathcal{T}\geqslant 0$ is not irreducible. First, we shall use a perturbation argument to deduce that $\rho(\mathcal{T})$ is a eigenvalue of $\mathcal{T}$ corresponding to a nonnegative eigenvector satisfying \eqref{noneigwkir}. Let $\mathcal{J}_{n,d}\in\mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$ be a tensor all the entries of which are $1$. Assume that $\epsilon>0$. Then $\mathcal{T}+\epsilon \mathcal{J}_{n,d}>0$. Hence there exists a positive probability vector $\mathbf{u}(\epsilon)$ so that \[(\mathcal{T}+\epsilon\mathcal{J}_{n,d})(\mathbf{u}(\epsilon))=\rho(\mathcal{T}+\epsilon \mathcal{J}_{n,d})\mathbf{u}(\epsilon)^{\circ(d-1)}.\] From the first characterization \eqref{minmaxrhoirchar} we deduce that $\rho(\mathcal{T}+\epsilon\mathcal{J}_{n,d})$ is a nondecreasing function on $(0,\infty)$. Since $\rho(\mathcal{S})$ is a continuous function in $\mathcal{S}\in \mathbb{C}^{n^{\times d}}_{sp}$ it follows that $\lim_{\epsilon\searrow 0}\rho(\mathcal{T}+\epsilon\mathcal{J}_{n,d})=\rho(\mathcal{T})$. Observe next that there exists a decreasing sequence $\epsilon_j>0, j\in\mathbb{N}$ converging to zero such that $\mathbf{u}(\epsilon_j)$ converge to a probability vector $\mathbf{v}=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)$. Since $\mathbf{u}(\epsilon_j)=(u_{1,j},\ldots,u_{n,j})^\top$ is an eigenvector of $\mathcal{T}+\epsilon_j\mathcal{J}_{n,d}$ corresponding to $\rho(\mathcal{T}+\epsilon_j\mathcal{J}_{n,d})$ we deduce \eqref{noneigwkir}. The results in \cite[\S3]{nuss86} yield that for any nonnegative tensor $\mathcal{T}$ with maximal nonnegative eigenvalue $\rho(\mathcal{T})$, the characterization \eqref{infmaxcharrho} holds. (To apply the results in \cite{nuss86} we need to consider the homogeneous map of degree one $\mathbf{u}\mapsto (\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{u}))^{\circ\frac{1}{d-1}}$ for $\mathbf{u}\geqslant \mathbf{0}$. Here for $\mathbf{u}=(u_1,\ldots,u_n)^\top\geqslant \mathbf{0}$ we denote by $\mathbf{u}^{\circ t}$ the vector $(u_1^t,\ldots,u_n^t)^\top$ for $t>0$. See for more details \cite{FGH}.) One can also use the above perturbation technique to deduce \eqref{infmaxcharrho}. The statements of the theorem for a weakly irreducible tensor $\mathcal{T}$ follow from~\cite[Corollary 4.2]{FGH}.
nodes.statement_short: Irreducible case from CPZ08; general case by perturbation T+eps J and compactness; Collatz-Wielandt via Nussbaum; weakly irreducible case from FGH.
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Irreducible case
nodes.statement: Suppose first that $\mathcal{T}$ is irreducible. Then the results in \cite{CPZ08} show that any nonnegative eigenvector is positive, and that this eigenvector is unique up to a scalar factor. It corresponds to a positive eigenvalue which is the spectral radius of $\mathcal{T}$. Furthermore, the characterization in \eqref{minmaxrhoirchar} holds.
nodes.statement_short: Irreducible case: cite CPZ08 for positivity, uniqueness and the min-max formula.
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Reducible case by perturbation
nodes.statement: Assume that $\mathcal{T}\geqslant 0$ is not irreducible. First, we shall use a perturbation argument to deduce that $\rho(\mathcal{T})$ is a eigenvalue of $\mathcal{T}$ corresponding to a nonnegative eigenvector satisfying \eqref{noneigwkir}. Let $\mathcal{J}_{n,d}\in\mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$ be a tensor all the entries of which are $1$. Assume that $\epsilon>0$. Then $\mathcal{T}+\epsilon \mathcal{J}_{n,d}>0$. Hence there exists a positive probability vector $\mathbf{u}(\epsilon)$ so that \[(\mathcal{T}+\epsilon\mathcal{J}_{n,d})(\mathbf{u}(\epsilon))=\rho(\mathcal{T}+\epsilon \mathcal{J}_{n,d})\mathbf{u}(\epsilon)^{\circ(d-1)}.\] From the first characterization \eqref{minmaxrhoirchar} we deduce that $\rho(\mathcal{T}+\epsilon\mathcal{J}_{n,d})$ is a nondecreasing function on $(0,\infty)$. Since $\rho(\mathcal{S})$ is a continuous function in $\mathcal{S}\in \mathbb{C}^{n^{\times d}}_{sp}$ it follows that $\lim_{\epsilon\searrow 0}\rho(\mathcal{T}+\epsilon\mathcal{J}_{n,d})=\rho(\mathcal{T})$. Observe next that there exists a decreasing sequence $\epsilon_j>0, j\in\mathbb{N}$ converging to zero such that $\mathbf{u}(\epsilon_j)$ converge to a probability vector $\mathbf{v}=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)$. Since $\mathbf{u}(\epsilon_j)=(u_{1,j},\ldots,u_{n,j})^\top$ is an eigenvector of $\mathcal{T}+\epsilon_j\mathcal{J}_{n,d}$ corresponding to $\rho(\mathcal{T}+\epsilon_j\mathcal{J}_{n,d})$ we deduce \eqref{noneigwkir}.
nodes.statement_short: Perturb by eps J, use monotonicity and continuity, and pass to a convergent subsequence of eigenvectors.
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Collatz-Wielandt via Nussbaum
nodes.statement: The results in \cite[\S3]{nuss86} yield that for any nonnegative tensor $\mathcal{T}$ with maximal nonnegative eigenvalue $\rho(\mathcal{T})$, the characterization \eqref{infmaxcharrho} holds. (To apply the results in \cite{nuss86} we need to consider the homogeneous map of degree one $\mathbf{u}\mapsto (\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{u}))^{\circ\frac{1}{d-1}}$ for $\mathbf{u}\geqslant \mathbf{0}$. Here for $\mathbf{u}=(u_1,\ldots,u_n)^\top\geqslant \mathbf{0}$ we denote by $\mathbf{u}^{\circ t}$ the vector $(u_1^t,\ldots,u_n^t)^\top$ for $t>0$. See for more details \cite{FGH}.) One can also use the above perturbation technique to deduce \eqref{infmaxcharrho}.
nodes.statement_short: Nussbaum's nonlinear Collatz-Wielandt formula gives (3.10).
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Weakly irreducible case
nodes.statement: The statements of the theorem for a weakly irreducible tensor $\mathcal{T}$ follow from~\cite[Corollary 4.2]{FGH}.
nodes.statement_short: Weakly irreducible case from FGH Corollary 4.2.
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Positive eigenvector u
nodes.statement: We denote by $\mathbf{u}=(u_1,\ldots,u_n)^\top>\mathbf{0}$ the corresponding positive eigenvector.
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Eigen-system map G(z, lambda, R)
nodes.statement: Thus, we have a system of $n$ nonlinear equations in $n$ unknowns, consisting of $z_1,\ldots,z_{n-1}$, the entries of $\mathbf{z}=(z_1,\ldots,z_{n-1},1)^\top\in\mathbb{C}^n$ and of the eigenvalue $\lambda$, given by \begin{equation} \mathbf{G}(\mathbf{z},\lambda,\mathcal{R})=\mathbf{0}, \quad \mathbf{G}(\mathbf{z},\lambda,\mathcal{R}):=\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{z})-\lambda\mathbf{z}^{\circ(d-1)} \enspace . \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Eigen-system equation (3.14)
nodes.statement: \mathbf{G}(\mathbf{z},\lambda,\mathcal{R})=\mathbf{0}, \quad \mathbf{G}(\mathbf{z},\lambda,\mathcal{R}):=\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{z})-\lambda\mathbf{z}^{\circ(d-1)} \enspace .
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors
nodes.label: eigeq

nodes.name: Differential map DT(x)
nodes.statement: First observe that \begin{equation} \mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y})=\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x})+D \mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{y} + O(\|\mathbf{y}\|^2), \quad D \mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x}):=(d-1)\mathcal{T}\times \otimes^{d-2}\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}, \end{equation} where $D \mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x})$ denotes the differential map of $\mathcal{T}$ at point $\mathbf{x}$.
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: First-order expansion of T(x) (3.15)
nodes.statement: \mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x}+\mathbf{y})=\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x})+D \mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{y} + O(\|\mathbf{y}\|^2), \quad D \mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x}):=(d-1)\mathcal{T}\times \otimes^{d-2}\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n},
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors
nodes.label: partderT

nodes.name: DT(u) is irreducible
nodes.statement: Second, assume that $\mathcal{T}\in\mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$ is weakly irreducible. Assume \eqref{poseigvec} holds. Then $D\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{u})\in \mathbb{R}_+^{n\times n}$ is an irreducible matrix satisfying \begin{equation} D\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{u})\mathbf{u}=(d-1)\rho(\mathcal{T})\mathbf{u}^{\circ(d-1)}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors
assumptions: assume that $\mathcal{T}\in\mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$ is weakly irreducible
conclusions: $D\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{u})\in \mathbb{R}_+^{n\times n}$ is an irreducible matrix satisfying

nodes.name: DT(u)u identity (3.16)
nodes.statement: D\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{u})\mathbf{u}=(d-1)\rho(\mathcal{T})\mathbf{u}^{\circ(d-1)}.
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors
nodes.label: pratTuid

nodes.name: Diagonal matrix diag(x)
nodes.statement: For a vector $\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\in \mathbb{R}^n$ denote by $\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{x})\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times n}$ the diagonal matrix $\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$.
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Matrix A = diag(u)^{-(d-2)} DT(u)
nodes.statement: Set \begin{equation} A:=\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{u})^{-(d-2)}D\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{u}), \quad\textrm{where }\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{u})=\rho(T)\mathbf{u}^{\circ (d-1)}, \mathbf{u}>\mathbf{0}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Definition of A (3.17)
nodes.statement: A:=\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{u})^{-(d-2)}D\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{u}), \quad\textrm{where }\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{u})=\rho(T)\mathbf{u}^{\circ (d-1)}, \mathbf{u}>\mathbf{0}.
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors
nodes.label: defATu

nodes.name: A is irreducible
nodes.statement: Since $D\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{u})$ is irreducible and $\mathbf{u}>0$, it follows that $A$ is an irreducible matrix.
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Left Perron vector w
nodes.statement: Furthermore, there exists a unique vector $\mathbf{0}<\mathbf{w}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ such that the following conditions hold \begin{equation} A\mathbf{u}=(d-1)\rho(\mathcal{T})\mathbf{u}, \quad A^\top\mathbf{w}=(d-1)\rho(\mathcal{T})\mathbf{w},\quad\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{u}=1. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Perron vectors of A (3.18)
nodes.statement: A\mathbf{u}=(d-1)\rho(\mathcal{T})\mathbf{u}, \quad A^\top\mathbf{w}=(d-1)\rho(\mathcal{T})\mathbf{w},\quad\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{u}=1.
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors
nodes.label: defpropA

nodes.name: First variation of the spectral radius
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{T}=[t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]\in\mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$ be weakly irreducible. \begin{enumerate} \item Assume that \eqref{poseigvec} holds. Then, there exists analytic functions $\mathbf{z}(\mathcal{R})$ and $\lambda(\mathcal{R})$ in the $n^d$ entries of $\mathcal{R}\in\mathbb{C}^{n^{\times d}}_{ps}$, defined in the neighborhood of $\mathcal{T}$, satisfying $\mathbf{z}(\mathcal{T})=\mathbf{u}$ and $\lambda(\mathcal{T})=\rho(\mathcal{T})$. \item Furthermore, let $\mathcal{S}=[s_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]\in \mathbb{R}^{n^{\times d}}_{ps}$ be such that $s_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}\geqslant 0$ if $t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}=0$. Then, for a small $\epsilon\geqslant 0$, one has the following expansion \begin{equation} \rho(\mathcal{T}+\epsilon\mathcal{S})=\rho(\mathcal{T})+\epsilon \mathbf{w}^\top \mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{u})^{-(d-2)}\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{u}) +O(\epsilon^2), \end{equation} where $\mathbf{w}$ is the positive vector defined in \eqref{defpropA}. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: The Perron eigenpair depends analytically on the tensor, and d rho(T+eps S)/d eps = w^T diag(u)^{-(d-2)} S(u).
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors
assumptions: let $\mathcal{S}=[s_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]\in \mathbb{R}^{n^{\times d}}_{ps}$ be such that $s_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}\geqslant 0$ if $t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}=0$
conclusions: there exists analytic functions $\mathbf{z}(\mathcal{R})$ and $\lambda(\mathcal{R})$ in the $n^d$ entries of $\mathcal{R}\in\mathbb{C}^{n^{\times d}}_{ps}$, defined in the neighborhood of $\mathcal{T}$, satisfying $\mathbf{z}(\mathcal{T})=\mathbf{u}$ and $\lambda(\mathcal{T})=\rho(\mathcal{T})$
for a small $\epsilon\geqslant 0$, one has the following expansion
nodes.label: pertspecrad

nodes.name: First-order expansion of rho (3.19)
nodes.statement: \rho(\mathcal{T}+\epsilon\mathcal{S})=\rho(\mathcal{T})+\epsilon \mathbf{w}^\top \mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{u})^{-(d-2)}\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{u}) +O(\epsilon^2),
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors
nodes.label: rhoTpert

nodes.name: Proof of the first variation formula
nodes.statement_short: Implicit function theorem: the Jacobian has rank n by Perron-Frobenius for A. Then compare first-order coefficients and multiply by w^T.
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Reduce to a rank condition
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{z},\lambda,\mathcal{R})$ be defined as in \eqref{eigeq}, where $\mathbf{z}=(z_1,\ldots,z_{n-1},1)^\top$. We next show that $D_{\mathbf{z},\lambda}\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{u},\rho(\mathcal{T}),\mathcal{T})$, i.e.\ the Jacobian of $\mathbf{G}$ with respect to $(\mathbf{z}, \lambda)$ at the point $(\mathbf{u},\rho(\mathcal{T}),\mathcal{T})$, has rank $n$.
nodes.statement_short: Goal: the Jacobian of G in (z, lambda) has rank n.
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Compute the Jacobian B
nodes.statement: The derivative of $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{z})-\lambda\mathbf{z}^{\circ(d-1)}$ with respect to the variable $z_i$ gives the $i$-th column of the matrix $D\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{z})-(d-1)\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{z})^{d-2}$ for $i=1,\ldots,n-1$. The derivative of $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{z})-\lambda\mathbf{z}^{\circ(d-1)}$ with respect to $\lambda$ gives the column $-\mathbf{z}^{\circ{d-1}}$. So the matrix $B:=D_{\mathbf{z},\lambda}\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{u},\rho(\mathcal{T}),\mathcal{T})\in\mathbb{R}_+^{n\times n}$ is given as follows. Its first $n-1$ columns are the first $n-1$ columns of $D\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{u})-(d-1)\rho(\mathcal{T})\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{u})^{d-2}$. The last column of $B$ is $-\mathbf{u}^{d-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Compute the columns of the Jacobian B.
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Rank of B via Perron-Frobenius
nodes.statement: Let $C:=\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{u})^{-(d-2)}B$. Then the first $n-1$ columns of $C$ are the first $n-1$ columns of $A-(d-1)\rho(\mathcal{T})I$, where $A$ is defined in \eqref{defATu}. The last column of $C$ is $-\mathbf{u}$. The Perron-Frobenius theorem yields that $\rho(A)=(d-1)\rho(\mathcal{T})$. Moreover, since $A$ is irreducible, the eigenspace of $A$ associated to the spectral radius of $A$ is of dimension $1$. As $(A-(d-1)\rho(\mathcal{T})I)\mathbf{u}=0$, we deduce that the unique linear combination of the columns of $A-(d-1)\rho(\mathcal{T})I$, up to a nonzero scalar, which is a zero vector, is given by the coordinates of $\mathbf{u}$. Since $\mathbf{u}_{n}\neq 0$, it follows that the first $n-1$ columns of $A-(d-1)\rho(\mathcal{T})I$ are linearly independent. From the definition of $\mathbf{w}>\mathbf{0}$ in \eqref{defpropA} it follows that the first $n-1$ columns of $A-(d-1)\rho(\mathcal{T})I$ form a basis to the subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$ orthogonal to the vector $\mathbf{w}$. By the definition $\mathbf{w}^\top \mathbf{u}=1$. Hence $\mathbf{u}$ is not a linear combination of the first $n-1$ columns of $A-(d-1)\rho(\mathcal{T})I$. So the columns of $C$ are linearly independent, i.e.\ $\mathrm{rank\;} C=n$. Therefore $\mathrm{rank\;} B=n$.
nodes.statement_short: Rescale to C and use Perron-Frobenius for A to show rank C = n.
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Implicit function theorem
nodes.statement: Since $\mathbf{G}(\mathbf{z},\lambda,\mathcal{R})$ is analytic in $(\mathbf{z},\lambda,\mathcal{R})$ the implicit function theorem implies that there exists analytic functions $\mathbf{z}(\mathcal{R}),\lambda(\mathcal{R})$ in the $n{n+d-2\choose d-1}$ entries of $\mathcal{R}\in\mathbb{C}^{n^{\times d}}_{ps}$ in the neighborhood of $\mathcal{T}$ satisfying $\mathbf{z}(\mathcal{T})=\mathbf{u},\lambda(\mathcal{T})=\rho(\mathcal{T})$.
nodes.statement_short: Implicit function theorem gives analytic z(R), lambda(R).
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Perturbation direction S
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{S}=[s_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]\in \mathbb{R}^{n^{\times d}}_{ps}$ such that $s_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}\geqslant 0$ if $t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}=0$. Assume $a>0$ satisfies the condition that $t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}+as_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}>0$ if $t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}>0$. Then $\mathcal{T}+\epsilon\mathcal{S}\in\mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$ is weakly irreducible for $\epsilon\in[0,a]$. Thus, the functions $\lambda(\mathcal{T}+\epsilon \mathcal{S})$ and $\mathbf{z}(\mathcal{T}+\epsilon\mathcal{S})$ of the parameter $\epsilon$ are analytic in some small open disc $|\epsilon|<r\leqslant a$, and $\lambda(\mathcal{T}+\epsilon \mathcal{S})=\rho(\mathcal{T}+\epsilon\mathcal{S})$ for $\epsilon \in [0,r)$.
nodes.statement_short: Fix S; T + eps S stays weakly irreducible, so lambda = rho along the path.
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: First-order coefficient
nodes.statement_short: Expand to first order and multiply by diag(u)^{-(d-2)}.
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Extract mu with w
nodes.statement: We now multiply from the left by the vector $\mathbf{w}^\top$. We finally use \eqref{defpropA} to deduce $\mu=\mathbf{w}^\top \mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{u})^{-(d-2)}\mathcal{S}(\mathbf{u})$. This establishes \eqref{rhoTpert}.
nodes.statement_short: Multiply by w^T to obtain the derivative formula (3.19).
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Multiplicativity of the spectral radius under Kronecker product
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{E}\in\mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{m^{\times d}},\mathcal{F}\in\mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$. Then $\rho(\mathcal{E})\rho(\mathcal{F})=\rho(\mathcal{E}\otimes_{\mathop{\mathrm{Kr}}\nolimits}\mathcal{F})$. Suppose furthermore that $m=n$. Then \begin{equation} \rho(\mathcal{E}\circ\mathcal{F})\leqslant \rho(\mathcal{E})\rho(\mathcal{F}) \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors
nodes.label: specradprodeq

nodes.name: Hadamard product spectral radius inequality (3.20)
nodes.statement: \rho(\mathcal{E}\circ\mathcal{F})\leqslant \rho(\mathcal{E})\rho(\mathcal{F})
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors
nodes.label: specradcircin

nodes.name: Proof of Kronecker multiplicativity
nodes.statement: Assume that $\mathcal{E}>0,\mathcal{F}>0$. Let $\mathbf{y}>\mathbf{0},\mathbf{x}>\mathbf{0}$ be the positive eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalues $\rho(\mathcal{E}),\rho(\mathcal{F})$ respectively. Then $\rho(\mathcal{E})\rho(\mathcal{F})$ is a positive eigenvalue of $\mathcal{E}\otimes_{\mathop{\mathrm{Kr}}\nolimits}\mathcal{F}$ corresponding to the positive eigenvalue $\mathbf{y}\otimes\mathbf{x}$. The results of \cite{CPZ08} yield the equality $\rho(\mathcal{E})\rho(\mathcal{F})=\rho(\mathcal{E}\otimes_{\mathop{\mathrm{Kr}}\nolimits}\mathcal{F})$. Clearly Characterization \eqref{infmaxcharrho} yields the inequality \eqref{specradcircin}. The results for nonnegative $\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F}$ is derived using the continuity argument as in the proof of Theorem \ref{propsecradten}.
nodes.statement_short: Positive case via product of Perron eigenvectors and CPZ08 uniqueness; Hadamard bound by Collatz-Wielandt; general case by continuity.
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Positive eigenvectors of E and F
nodes.statement: Assume that $\mathcal{E}>0,\mathcal{F}>0$. Let $\mathbf{y}>\mathbf{0},\mathbf{x}>\mathbf{0}$ be the positive eigenvectors corresponding to the eigenvalues $\rho(\mathcal{E}),\rho(\mathcal{F})$ respectively. Then $\rho(\mathcal{E})\rho(\mathcal{F})$ is a positive eigenvalue of $\mathcal{E}\otimes_{\mathop{\mathrm{Kr}}\nolimits}\mathcal{F}$ corresponding to the positive eigenvalue $\mathbf{y}\otimes\mathbf{x}$.
nodes.statement_short: For positive E, F the Kronecker product of eigenvectors is a positive eigenvector.
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Equality via CPZ08
nodes.statement: The results of \cite{CPZ08} yield the equality $\rho(\mathcal{E})\rho(\mathcal{F})=\rho(\mathcal{E}\otimes_{\mathop{\mathrm{Kr}}\nolimits}\mathcal{F})$.
nodes.statement_short: CPZ08 uniqueness yields the multiplicativity.
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Hadamard inequality
nodes.statement: Clearly Characterization \eqref{infmaxcharrho} yields the inequality \eqref{specradcircin}.
nodes.statement_short: Collatz-Wielandt gives the Hadamard product bound.
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Continuity argument
nodes.statement: The results for nonnegative $\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F}$ is derived using the continuity argument as in the proof of Theorem \ref{propsecradten}.
nodes.statement_short: Extend to nonnegative tensors by continuity.
nodes.section: 3.4 Spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Hadamard power of a tensor
nodes.statement: Given a tensor $\mathcal{A}=[a_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]\in \mathbb{R}_{pr,+}^{\mathbf{m}}$ and a real nonnegative number $p$, we set $\mathcal{A}^{\circ p}:=[a_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}^p]\in \mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{\mathbf{m}}$.
nodes.section: 4 Logconvexity of the spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Generalized Kingman inequality for tensors
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{F}=[f_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}],\mathcal{G}=[g_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]\in\mathbb{R}_{pr,+}^{n^{\times d}}$. Then \begin{equation} \rho(\mathcal{F}^{\circ \alpha}\circ\mathcal{G}^{\circ\beta})\leqslant (\rho(\mathcal{F}))^\alpha (\rho(\mathcal{G}))^\beta,\qquad \alpha,\beta> 0, \alpha+\beta=1. \end{equation} Assume that $\mathcal{F}^{\circ \alpha}\circ\mathcal{G}^{\circ\beta}$ is weakly irreducible. Let $\mathbf{u}=(u_1,\ldots,u_n)^\top$ and $\mathbf{v}=(v_1,\ldots,v_n)^\top$ be the positive eigenvectors of $\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{G}$: $\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{u})=\rho(T)\mathbf{u}^{\circ(d-1) }, \mathcal{G}(\mathbf{v})=\rho(\mathcal{G})\mathbf{v}^{\circ(d-1)}$. Then equality in the above inequality holds if and only if the following conditions are satisfied. There exists $\mathbf{a}=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)^\top >0$ such that \begin{equation} f_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}u_{i_2}\cdots u_{i_d}=a_{i_1}g_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}v_{i_2}\cdots v_{i_d} \quad \textrm{for all } i_1,\ldots,i_d\in[n]. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: rho(F^a o G^b) <= rho(F)^a rho(G)^b for a+b=1, with equality characterized by a diagonal-scaling condition.
nodes.section: 4 Logconvexity of the spectral radius of nonnegative tensors
conclusions: equality in the above inequality holds if and only if the following conditions are satisfied
equality in the above inequality holds if and only if the following conditions are satisfied

nodes.label: genkinin

nodes.name: Kingman-type inequality (4.1)
nodes.statement: \rho(\mathcal{F}^{\circ \alpha}\circ\mathcal{G}^{\circ\beta})\leqslant (\rho(\mathcal{F}))^\alpha (\rho(\mathcal{G}))^\beta,\qquad \alpha,\beta> 0, \alpha+\beta=1.
nodes.section: 4 Logconvexity of the spectral radius of nonnegative tensors
nodes.label: genkinin1

nodes.name: Equality condition (4.2)
nodes.statement: f_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}u_{i_2}\cdots u_{i_d}=a_{i_1}g_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}v_{i_2}\cdots v_{i_d} \quad \textrm{for all } i_1,\ldots,i_d\in[n].
nodes.section: 4 Logconvexity of the spectral radius of nonnegative tensors
nodes.label: eqcondlogconsr

nodes.name: Proof of the generalized Kingman inequality
nodes.statement: Assume that $\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{G}$ are weakly irreducible. Let $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{u}^{\circ \alpha}\circ\mathbf{v}^{\circ\beta}$. H\"older's inequality for $p=\alpha^{-1}, q=\beta^{-1}$ yields \begin{eqnarray*} \sum_{i_2,\ldots,i_d\in[n]} f_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}^{\alpha}g_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}^{\beta}u_{i_1}^{\alpha}v_{i_1}^{\beta}\ldots u_{i_d}^{\alpha}v_{i_d}^{\beta}= \sum_{i_2,\ldots,i_d\in[n]} (f_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}u_{i_1}\ldots u_{i_d})^{\alpha}(g_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}v_{i_1}\ldots v_{i_d})^{\beta}\\ \leqslant (\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{u})_{i_1})^{\alpha}(\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{v})_{i_1})^{\beta}=(\rho(\mathcal{F})^{\alpha}u_{i_1}^{(d-1)\alpha})(\rho(\mathcal{G})^{\beta}v_{i_1}^{(d-1)\beta})= (\rho(\mathcal{F})^{\alpha}\rho(\mathcal{G})^{\beta})x_{i_1}^{d-1}. \end{eqnarray*} So \[\rho(\mathcal{F}^{\alpha}\circ\mathcal{G}^{\beta})(\mathbf{x})\leqslant (\rho(\mathcal{F})^{\alpha}\rho(\mathcal{G})^{\beta})\mathbf{x}^{\circ(d-1)}.\] Use \eqref{infmaxcharrho} to deduce \eqref{genkinin1}. We now discuss the equality in \eqref{genkinin1}. Suppose that $\mathcal{R}:=\mathcal{F}^{\circ \alpha}\circ\mathcal{G}^{\circ\beta}$ is weakly irreducible. Then $\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{G}$ are weakly irreducible. Assume that equality holds in \eqref{genkinin1}. In view of the second part of the characterization \eqref{minmaxrhoirchar} it follows that $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{u}^{\circ\alpha}\circ\mathbf{v}^{\circ\beta}$ is the eigenvector of $\mathcal{R}$. The equality case of H\"older inequality yields \eqref{eqcondlogconsr}. Conversely, if \eqref{eqcondlogconsr} holds then $\mathbf{x}$ is a positive eigenvector of $\mathcal{R}$ corresponding to $\rho(\mathcal{R})=\rho(\mathcal{F})^{\alpha}\rho(\mathcal{G})^{\beta}$. To deduce the inequality \eqref{genkinin1} for any nonnegative $\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G}$ we use the continuity argument. Let $\epsilon>0$ and $0<\mathcal{J}_{n,d}\in \mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$. Then \eqref{genkinin1} hods for $\mathcal{F}(\epsilon):=\mathcal{F}+\epsilon \mathcal{J}_{n,d}, \mathcal{G}(\epsilon):=\mathcal{G}+\epsilon\mathcal{J}_{n,d}$. Now let $\epsilon\searrow 0$ to deduce \eqref{genkinin1}.
nodes.statement_short: Hoelder's inequality on the Perron eigenvectors plus Collatz-Wielandt; equality case of Hoelder; continuity for the general case.
nodes.section: 4 Logconvexity of the spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Hoelder bound
nodes.statement: Assume that $\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{G}$ are weakly irreducible. Let $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{u}^{\circ \alpha}\circ\mathbf{v}^{\circ\beta}$. H\"older's inequality for $p=\alpha^{-1}, q=\beta^{-1}$ yields \begin{eqnarray*} \sum_{i_2,\ldots,i_d\in[n]} f_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}^{\alpha}g_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}^{\beta}u_{i_1}^{\alpha}v_{i_1}^{\beta}\ldots u_{i_d}^{\alpha}v_{i_d}^{\beta}= \sum_{i_2,\ldots,i_d\in[n]} (f_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}u_{i_1}\ldots u_{i_d})^{\alpha}(g_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}v_{i_1}\ldots v_{i_d})^{\beta}\\ \leqslant (\mathcal{F}(\mathbf{u})_{i_1})^{\alpha}(\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{v})_{i_1})^{\beta}=(\rho(\mathcal{F})^{\alpha}u_{i_1}^{(d-1)\alpha})(\rho(\mathcal{G})^{\beta}v_{i_1}^{(d-1)\beta})= (\rho(\mathcal{F})^{\alpha}\rho(\mathcal{G})^{\beta})x_{i_1}^{d-1}. \end{eqnarray*} So \[\rho(\mathcal{F}^{\alpha}\circ\mathcal{G}^{\beta})(\mathbf{x})\leqslant (\rho(\mathcal{F})^{\alpha}\rho(\mathcal{G})^{\beta})\mathbf{x}^{\circ(d-1)}.\] Use \eqref{infmaxcharrho} to deduce \eqref{genkinin1}.
nodes.statement_short: Hoelder's inequality on u^a o v^b and Collatz-Wielandt give (4.1) for weakly irreducible F, G.
nodes.section: 4 Logconvexity of the spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Equality forces condition (4.2)
nodes.statement: We now discuss the equality in \eqref{genkinin1}. Suppose that $\mathcal{R}:=\mathcal{F}^{\circ \alpha}\circ\mathcal{G}^{\circ\beta}$ is weakly irreducible. Then $\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{G}$ are weakly irreducible. Assume that equality holds in \eqref{genkinin1}. In view of the second part of the characterization \eqref{minmaxrhoirchar} it follows that $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{u}^{\circ\alpha}\circ\mathbf{v}^{\circ\beta}$ is the eigenvector of $\mathcal{R}$. The equality case of H\"older inequality yields \eqref{eqcondlogconsr}.
nodes.statement_short: Equality forces x to be the eigenvector, and Hoelder's equality case gives (4.2).
nodes.section: 4 Logconvexity of the spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Condition (4.2) gives equality
nodes.statement: Conversely, if \eqref{eqcondlogconsr} holds then $\mathbf{x}$ is a positive eigenvector of $\mathcal{R}$ corresponding to $\rho(\mathcal{R})=\rho(\mathcal{F})^{\alpha}\rho(\mathcal{G})^{\beta}$.
nodes.statement_short: Conversely (4.2) makes x a positive eigenvector.
nodes.section: 4 Logconvexity of the spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Continuity argument
nodes.statement: To deduce the inequality \eqref{genkinin1} for any nonnegative $\mathcal{F},\mathcal{G}$ we use the continuity argument. Let $\epsilon>0$ and $0<\mathcal{J}_{n,d}\in \mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$. Then \eqref{genkinin1} hods for $\mathcal{F}(\epsilon):=\mathcal{F}+\epsilon \mathcal{J}_{n,d}, \mathcal{G}(\epsilon):=\mathcal{G}+\epsilon\mathcal{J}_{n,d}$. Now let $\epsilon\searrow 0$ to deduce \eqref{genkinin1}.
nodes.statement_short: Perturb by eps J and let eps -> 0.
nodes.section: 4 Logconvexity of the spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Logconvex function
nodes.statement: Let $D\subset \mathbb{R}^m$ be a convex set. A function $f:D\to \mathbb{R}_+$ is called \emph{logconvex} if the function $\log f:D\to [-\infty,\infty)$ is continuous and convex.
nodes.section: 4 Logconvexity of the spectral radius of nonnegative tensors
differentia: the function $\log f:D\to [-\infty,\infty)$ is continuous and convex

nodes.name: Logconvex tensor-valued function
nodes.statement: A vector function $\mathcal{T}:D\to \mathbb{R}^{\mathbf{m}}$ is called logconvex if each entry $t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}:D\to \mathbb{R}_+$ is logconvex.
nodes.section: 4 Logconvexity of the spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Proof of log-convexity of the spectral radius
nodes.statement: This lemma implies the following generalization of Kingman's theorem for the spectral radius of matrices with logconvex entries.
nodes.statement_short: Follows from Lemma 6 (generalized Kingman inequality).
nodes.section: 4 Logconvexity of the spectral radius of nonnegative tensors

nodes.name: Log-convexity of the spectral radius (Kingman's theorem for tensors)
nodes.statement: Let $D\subset \mathbb{R}^m$ be a convex set. Assume that $\mathcal{T}:D\to \mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$ is logconvex. Then $\rho(\mathcal{T}):D\to\mathbb{R}_+$ is logconvex.
nodes.section: 4 Logconvexity of the spectral radius of nonnegative tensors
nodes.label: logconvsr

nodes.name: Row scaling diag(y) o T
nodes.statement: For a tensor $\mathcal{T}=[t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]\in \mathbb{F}^{n^{\times d}}$ and a vector $\mathbf{y}=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)^\top \in\mathbb{F}^{n}$ we define $\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{y})\circ \mathcal{T}$ to be the tensor $[y_{i_1}t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]\in \mathbb{F}^{n^{\times d}}$.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Friedland-Karlin inequality for tensors
nodes.statement: Assume that $\mathcal{T}\in \mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$ is a weakly irreducible tensor. Let $A,\mathbf{u},\mathbf{w}$ be given by \eqref{defATu} and \eqref{defpropA}. Assume that $\mathbf{y}=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)^\top>0$. Then \begin{equation} \rho(\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{y})\circ \mathcal{T})\geqslant \rho(\mathcal{T})\prod_{i=1}^n y_i^{u_iw_i}. \end{equation} Assume furthermore that $\mathcal{T}$ is a symmetric tensor and {{$\sum_{i=1}^n u_i^d=1$}}. Then \begin{equation} \rho(\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{y})\circ \mathcal{T})\geqslant \rho(\mathcal{T})\prod_{i=1}^n y_i^{u_i^d}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: rho(diag(y) o T) >= rho(T) prod y_i^{u_i w_i}; for symmetric T the exponents become u_i^d.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality
assumptions: Assume that $\mathcal{T}\in \mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$ is a weakly irreducible tensor.
Assume furthermore that $\mathcal{T}$ is a symmetric tensor and {{$\sum_{i=1}^n u_i^d=1$}}.
Assume furthermore that $\mathcal{T}$ is a symmetric tensor and {{$\sum_{i=1}^n u_i^d=1$}}.

nodes.label: FKtens

nodes.name: Friedland-Karlin inequality (5.1)
nodes.statement: \rho(\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{y})\circ \mathcal{T})\geqslant \rho(\mathcal{T})\prod_{i=1}^n y_i^{u_iw_i}.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality
nodes.label: frikar

nodes.name: Symmetric Friedland-Karlin inequality (5.2)
nodes.statement: \rho(\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{y})\circ \mathcal{T})\geqslant \rho(\mathcal{T})\prod_{i=1}^n y_i^{u_i^d}.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality
nodes.label: frikarsym

nodes.name: Proof of the Friedland-Karlin inequality for tensors
nodes.statement: For $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ let $e^{\mathbf{x}}=(e^{x_1},\ldots,e^{x_n})^\top$. Then $\rho(\mathbf{x})=\rho(\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(e^{\mathbf{x}})\circ \mathcal{T})$ is a log-convex function in $\mathbf{x}$ see \S\ref{sec:logconv}. Hence $\lambda(\mathbf{x}):=(\rho(\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(e^{\mathbf{x}})\circ \mathcal{T}))^{\frac{1}{d-1}}$ is also log-convex. The log-convexity property yields $$\log\lambda(\mathbf{x})\geqslant \log\lambda(\mathbf{0})+\mathbf{x}^\top (D\log\lambda)(\mathbf{0})=\log\lambda(\mathbf{0})+\frac{1}{\lambda(\mathbf{0})}\mathbf{x}^\top(D\lambda)(\mathbf{0}).$$ Note that $\lambda(\mathbf{0})=\rho(\mathcal{T})^{\frac{1}{d-1}}$. Now use Theorem \ref{pertspecrad}, together with $e^{x_i}=1+x_i + O(x_i^2)$, to show that $$\mathbf{x}^\top(D\lambda)(\mathbf{0})=\frac{\lambda_0}{d-1}\sum_{i=1}^n x_iu_iw_i.$$ So $\lambda(x)\geqslant \lambda_0 e^{\frac{1}{d-1}\sum_{i=1}^n x_iu_iw_i}$. Raise this to the power $d-1$ and let $y_i=e^{x_i}, i=1,\ldots,n$, to deduce \eqref{frikar}. Assume furthermore that $\mathcal{T}$ is symmetric. Then $\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{u}^{\circ (d-1)}$, where we have the normalization $\sum_{i=1}^n u_i^d=1$. Hence \eqref{frikar} is equivalent to \eqref{frikarsym}.
nodes.statement_short: Log-convexity of x -> rho(diag(e^x) o T) gives a tangent-line lower bound; the gradient comes from the first variation formula.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Log-convexity of the rescaled spectral radius
nodes.statement: For $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n$ let $e^{\mathbf{x}}=(e^{x_1},\ldots,e^{x_n})^\top$. Then $\rho(\mathbf{x})=\rho(\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(e^{\mathbf{x}})\circ \mathcal{T})$ is a log-convex function in $\mathbf{x}$ see \S\ref{sec:logconv}. Hence $\lambda(\mathbf{x}):=(\rho(\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(e^{\mathbf{x}})\circ \mathcal{T}))^{\frac{1}{d-1}}$ is also log-convex.
nodes.statement_short: x -> rho(diag(e^x) o T)^{1/(d-1)} is log-convex.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Tangent-line lower bound
nodes.statement: The log-convexity property yields $$\log\lambda(\mathbf{x})\geqslant \log\lambda(\mathbf{0})+\mathbf{x}^\top (D\log\lambda)(\mathbf{0})=\log\lambda(\mathbf{0})+\frac{1}{\lambda(\mathbf{0})}\mathbf{x}^\top(D\lambda)(\mathbf{0}).$$ Note that $\lambda(\mathbf{0})=\rho(\mathcal{T})^{\frac{1}{d-1}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Log-convexity gives a supporting-hyperplane lower bound at 0.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Gradient via first variation
nodes.statement: Now use Theorem \ref{pertspecrad}, together with $e^{x_i}=1+x_i + O(x_i^2)$, to show that $$\mathbf{x}^\top(D\lambda)(\mathbf{0})=\frac{\lambda_0}{d-1}\sum_{i=1}^n x_iu_iw_i.$$
nodes.statement_short: The first variation formula computes the gradient at 0.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Exponentiate
nodes.statement: So $\lambda(x)\geqslant \lambda_0 e^{\frac{1}{d-1}\sum_{i=1}^n x_iu_iw_i}$. Raise this to the power $d-1$ and let $y_i=e^{x_i}, i=1,\ldots,n$, to deduce \eqref{frikar}.
nodes.statement_short: Exponentiate and substitute y_i = e^{x_i} to get (5.1).
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Symmetric case
nodes.statement: Assume furthermore that $\mathcal{T}$ is symmetric. Then $\mathbf{w}=\mathbf{u}^{\circ (d-1)}$, where we have the normalization $\sum_{i=1}^n u_i^d=1$. Hence \eqref{frikar} is equivalent to \eqref{frikarsym}.
nodes.statement_short: For symmetric T, w = u^{[d-1]} so (5.1) becomes (5.2).
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Friedland-Karlin improved inequality for PSD matrices
nodes.statement: Theorem 4.1 in \cite{FK75} claims that if $T$ is an nonnegative irreducible symmetric matrix which is also a positive semi-definite then inequality \eqref{frikarsym} (with $d=2$) can be improved to \[\rho(\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{y})\circ T))\geqslant \rho(T)\sum_{i=1}^d y_i u_i^2.\]
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality
assumptions: $T$ is an nonnegative irreducible symmetric matrix which is also a positive semi-definite

nodes.name: Polynomial f and map F_i of a symmetric tensor
nodes.statement: {{Recall that that a symmetric tensor $\mathcal{T}$ is induced by a homogeneous polynomial $f(\mathbf{x})$ of degree $d$ \ref{subsec:homeigv}}}: {{\[f(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^\top \mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x}), \quad \mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x}) =\mathcal{T}\times(\otimes^{d-1}\mathbf{x})=\frac{1}{d}\nabla f(\mathbf{x})=(F_1(\mathbf{x}),\ldots,F_n(\mathbf{x}))^\top.\]}}
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Positive definite quadratic forms are strictly convex
nodes.statement: Observe next that $f(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}$ corresponds to a positive definite matrix if and only if $f$ is strictly convex.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality
conclusions: $f(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}$ corresponds to a positive definite matrix if and only if $f$ is strictly convex
equivalent_conditions: $f(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^\top A\mathbf{x}$ corresponds to a positive definite matrix

nodes.name: Positivity condition (5.3)
nodes.statement: f(\mathbf{x})>0 \textrm{ for all } \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{\mathbf{0}\}.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality
nodes.label: poscond

nodes.name: Positivity forces even degree
nodes.statement: Note that if $f(\mathbf{x})$ is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $d$ then the above condition can hold only if $d$ is an even integer.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality
assumptions: $f(\mathbf{x})$ is a homogeneous polynomial of degree $d$
conclusions: the above condition can hold only if $d$ is an even integer

nodes.name: Generalized Friedland-Karlin inequality for convex polynomials
nodes.statement_short: For a convex positive even-degree form, rho(diag(y) o T)^{1/(d-1)} is a max of a Rayleigh-type ratio, giving an improved Friedland-Karlin bound.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality
assumptions: Let $d$ be a positive even integer.
Let $f(\mathbf{x})$ be a homogeneous polynomial of degree $d$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$
The tensor $\mathcal{T}$ is nonnegative and weakly irreducible.
conclusions: If the Hessian of $f(\mathbf{x})$ is positive definite at each $\mathbf{x}\ne \mathbf{0}$ then equality holds iff $\mathbf{y}=c\mathbf{1}$.
nodes.label: genKFsc

nodes.name: Max characterization of rho(diag(y) o T) (5.4)
nodes.statement: \rho(\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{y})\circ \mathcal{T})^{\frac{1}{d-1}}=\max_{\mathbf{x}\ne \mathbf{0}} \frac{\sum_{i=1} y_i^{\frac{1}{d-1}}F_i(\mathbf{x})^{\frac{d}{d-1}}}{f(\mathbf{x})}.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality
nodes.label: maxcharrhoyT

nodes.name: Improved Friedland-Karlin inequality (5.5)
nodes.statement: \rho(\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{y})\circ \mathcal{T})\geqslant \rho(\mathcal{T})\left(\sum_{i=1}^n y_i^{\frac{1}{d-1}}{u_i^d}\right)^{d-1}.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality
nodes.label: frikarsym2

nodes.name: Proof of the generalized Friedland-Karlin inequality
nodes.statement_short: Match critical points of the ratio with eigenvectors of diag(y) o T via Euler's identities, then perturb by a strictly convex form. The key step identifies the maximal critical value with rho via Collatz-Wielandt.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Hessian entries and strict convexity assumption
nodes.statement: {{Let $F_{ij}=\frac{1}{d-1}\frac{\partial F_i}{\partial x_j}=\frac{1}{(d-1)d}\frac{\partial ^2\;\;\;\;\;\;}{\partial x_j\partial x_i}f$.}} We first assume that the Hessian $H(\mathbf{x})$ of $f(x)$ is positive definite for each $\mathbf{x}\ne \mathbf{0}$. Assume that $\mathbf{y}=(y_1,\ldots,y_n)^\top>\mathbf{0}$ is fixed.
nodes.statement_short: Define F_ij and first assume a positive definite Hessian.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Critical point equation
nodes.statement_short: Critical points of the ratio satisfy (5.6).
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Critical point condition (5.6)
nodes.statement: \sum_{i=1}^n y_i^{\frac{1}{d-1}} F_i(\mathbf{x})^{\frac{1}{d-1}}F_{ij}(\mathbf{x})=\lambda F_j(\mathbf{x}), \quad j\in [n], \mathbf{x}\ne \mathbf{0},\lambda\ne 0.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality
nodes.label: critpointcond

nodes.name: Eigenproblem for diag(y) o T
nodes.statement: Next we consider the following the eigenvalue problem for $\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{y})\circ\mathcal{T}$: \begin{equation} y_iF_i(\mathbf{x})=\mu \mathbf{x}^{\circ(d-1)}, \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{\mathbf{0}\}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Consider the eigenproblem (5.7).
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Eigenproblem for diag(y) o T (5.7)
nodes.statement: y_iF_i(\mathbf{x})=\mu \mathbf{x}^{\circ(d-1)}, \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n\setminus\{\mathbf{0}\}.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality
nodes.label: eigenvector

nodes.name: Positivity of mu
nodes.statement: Observe first that $\mu>0$. Indeed, Euler's formula yields that \[0<dF(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{i=1}^d x_i F_i(\mathbf{x})=\mu \sum_{i=1}^d y_i^{-1}x_i^d.\]
nodes.statement_short: Euler's formula shows mu > 0.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Eigenvectors are critical points
nodes.statement: We claim that each eigenvector satisfying \eqref{eigenvector} satisfies \eqref{critpointcond}. Indeed, \[F_i(\mathbf{x})^{\frac{1}{d-1}}= y_i^{-\frac{1}{d-1}}\mu^{\frac{1}{d-1}}x_i, \quad i\in[n].\] Observe next that $F_j$ is a homogeneous function of degree $d-1$. Furthermore $F_{ij}=F_{ji}$. Use Euler's formula to deduce \[ \sum_{i=1}^n y_i^{\frac{1}{d-1}} F_i(\mathbf{x})^{\frac{1}{d-1}}F_{ij}(\mathbf{x})=\mu^{\frac{1}{d-1}}\sum_{i=1}^n x_iF_{ji}(\mathbf{x})=\mu^{\frac{1}{d-1}}F_j(\mathbf{x}).\] Hence \eqref{critpointcond} holds with $\lambda=\mu^{\frac{1}{d-1}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Every eigenvector of (5.7) satisfies (5.6).
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Rewrite F_i
nodes.statement: Indeed, \[F_i(\mathbf{x})^{\frac{1}{d-1}}= y_i^{-\frac{1}{d-1}}\mu^{\frac{1}{d-1}}x_i, \quad i\in[n].\] Observe next that $F_j$ is a homogeneous function of degree $d-1$. Furthermore $F_{ij}=F_{ji}$.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite F_i^{1/(d-1)} via the eigen-equation; F_j is homogeneous and F_ij symmetric.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Apply Euler's formula
nodes.statement: Use Euler's formula to deduce \[ \sum_{i=1}^n y_i^{\frac{1}{d-1}} F_i(\mathbf{x})^{\frac{1}{d-1}}F_{ij}(\mathbf{x})=\mu^{\frac{1}{d-1}}\sum_{i=1}^n x_iF_{ji}(\mathbf{x})=\mu^{\frac{1}{d-1}}F_j(\mathbf{x}).\] Hence \eqref{critpointcond} holds with $\lambda=\mu^{\frac{1}{d-1}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Euler's formula yields (5.6) with lambda = mu^{1/(d-1)}.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Critical points are eigenvectors
nodes.statement: Assume now that \eqref{critpointcond} holds. We claim that \eqref{eigenvector} holds with $\mu=\lambda^{d-1}$. Indeed, Euler's identities yield that \[\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda x_i F_{ij}(\mathbf{x})=\lambda F_j(\mathbf{x}), \quad j\in[n].\] Since $H(\mathbf{x})=[F_{ij}(\mathbf{x})]$ is invertible it follows that $y_i^{\frac{1}{d-1}} F_i(\mathbf{x})^{\frac{1}{d-1}}=\lambda x_i$ for $i\in[d]$.
nodes.statement_short: Conversely critical points give eigenvectors with mu = lambda^{d-1}.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Euler identities
nodes.statement: Indeed, Euler's identities yield that \[\sum_{i=1}^n \lambda x_i F_{ij}(\mathbf{x})=\lambda F_j(\mathbf{x}), \quad j\in[n].\]
nodes.statement_short: Euler's identities for F_ij.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Invert the Hessian
nodes.statement: Since $H(\mathbf{x})=[F_{ij}(\mathbf{x})]$ is invertible it follows that $y_i^{\frac{1}{d-1}} F_i(\mathbf{x})^{\frac{1}{d-1}}=\lambda x_i$ for $i\in[d]$.
nodes.statement_short: Invertibility of the Hessian gives the eigen-equation.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Maximal critical value is rho
nodes.statement_short: Collatz-Wielandt shows the maximal critical value corresponds to rho(diag(y) o T), proving (5.4).
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Choose x = u
nodes.statement: To show \eqref{frikarsym2} choose $\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{u}$ in the maximum characterization \eqref{maxcharrhoyT}. Since $\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{y})\circ\mathcal{T}$ is weakly irreducible it follows that equality in \eqref{frikarsym2} is achieved if and only if $\mathbf{u}$ is the Perron-Frobenius eigenvalue of $\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{y})\circ\mathcal{T}$, i.e., $\mathbf{y}=c\mathbf{1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Plug x = u into (5.4) to get (5.5) and characterize equality.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Convex case by perturbation
nodes.statement: We now show \eqref{maxcharrhoyT} and \eqref{frikarsym2} assuming that $F(\mathbf{x})$ is convex but no longer necessarily strictly convex. So $H(\mathbf{x})$ is a positive semi-definite symmetric matrix. Consider \[G(\mathbf{x})=\sum_{i=1}^{2n-1} (\sum_{j=1}^n b_{ij}x_j)^d.\] Let $B=[b_{ij}]\in\mathbb{R}^{(2n-1)\times n}_{+}$. Assume that any $n$ rows of $B$ are linearly independent. It is straightforward to show that $G(\mathbf{x})$ satisfies all the assumptions of the theorem. Moreover $H(G)(x)$ is positive definite for $\mathbf{x}\ne \mathbf{0}$. Let $\mathcal{S}$ be the induced symmetric tensor by $G(\mathbf{x})$. Then for $\epsilon >0$, $\mathcal{T}(\epsilon)=\mathcal{T}+\epsilon \mathcal{S}$ satisfies the assumptions of the theorem. Furthermore $H(\mathcal{T}(\epsilon))(\mathbf{x})$ is positive definite for $\mathbf{x}\ne 0$. Hence the characterizations \eqref{maxcharrhoyT} and \eqref{frikarsym2} hold. Letting $\epsilon \to 0$ we deduce the theorem for $\mathcal{T}$.
nodes.statement_short: Perturb by a strictly convex form G and let eps -> 0.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Remark on replacing convexity by invertible Hessian
nodes.statement: The arguments of the proof of the Theorem \ref{genKFsc} apply if we replace the condition \emph{3} of Theorem \ref{genKFsc} by the condition that the Hessian of $F(\mathbf{x})$ is invertible for each $\mathbf{x}\ne \mathbf{0}$. For $d=2$, the condition \emph{2}, i.e., \eqref{poscond}, yields that $F$ is strictly convex. We do not know if the condition \eqref{poscond} and the condition that the Hessian of $F(\mathbf{x})$ is invertible implies that $F$ is strictly convex for an even $d>2$.
nodes.statement_short: The proof works with an invertible-Hessian condition instead of convexity; unknown whether this forces strict convexity for even d>2.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Does positivity plus invertible Hessian imply strict convexity?
nodes.statement: We do not know if the condition \eqref{poscond} and the condition that the Hessian of $F(\mathbf{x})$ is invertible implies that $F$ is strictly convex for an even $d>2$.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Min characterization of log rho (Friedland-Karlin Theorem 3.1 for tensors)
nodes.statement: Assume that $\mathcal{T}\in \mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$ is a weakly irreducible tensor. Then \begin{equation} \log \rho(\mathcal{T})=\min_{\mathbf{x}>0} \sum_{i=1}^n u_iw_i \log \frac{(\mathcal{T}\mathbf{x})_i}{x_i^{d-1}}. \end{equation} The equality holds if and only if $\mathbf{x}$ is the eigenvector $c\mathbf{u}, c>0$ of $\mathcal{T}$.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality
assumptions: Assume that $\mathcal{T}\in \mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$ is a weakly irreducible tensor.
conclusions: The equality holds if and only if $\mathbf{x}$ is the eigenvector $c\mathbf{u}, c>0$ of $\mathcal{T}$.
nodes.label: corFKtens

nodes.name: Min characterization of log rho (5.8)
nodes.statement: \log \rho(\mathcal{T})=\min_{\mathbf{x}>0} \sum_{i=1}^n u_iw_i \log \frac{(\mathcal{T}\mathbf{x})_i}{x_i^{d-1}}.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality
nodes.label: minrhoTchar

nodes.name: Proof of the min characterization of log rho
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{x}>\mathbf{0}$. Define $y_i=\frac{x_i^{d-1}}{\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x})_i}$. Then $(\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{y})\mathcal{T})(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^{\circ(d-1)}$. So $\rho(\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{y})\mathcal{T})=1$. Apply \eqref{frikar} to deduce the inequality $ \sum_{i=1}^n u_iw_i \log \frac{(\mathcal{T}\mathbf{x})_i}{x_i^{d-1}}\geqslant\log \rho(\mathcal{T})$. Equality holds if and only if $\mathbf{y}=c\mathbf{1}$, i.e.\ $\mathbf{x}=c\mathbf{u}$.
nodes.statement_short: Rescale by y_i = x_i^{d-1}/T(x)_i so the spectral radius is 1, then apply the Friedland-Karlin inequality.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Rescaling with spectral radius 1
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{x}>\mathbf{0}$. Define $y_i=\frac{x_i^{d-1}}{\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x})_i}$. Then $(\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{y})\mathcal{T})(\mathbf{x})=\mathbf{x}^{\circ(d-1)}$. So $\rho(\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(\mathbf{y})\mathcal{T})=1$.
nodes.statement_short: Define y_i = x_i^{d-1}/T(x)_i so diag(y)T has spectral radius 1.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Apply Friedland-Karlin
nodes.statement: Apply \eqref{frikar} to deduce the inequality $ \sum_{i=1}^n u_iw_i \log \frac{(\mathcal{T}\mathbf{x})_i}{x_i^{d-1}}\geqslant\log \rho(\mathcal{T})$.
nodes.statement_short: Friedland-Karlin inequality gives the lower bound on the sum.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Equality case
nodes.statement: Equality holds if and only if $\mathbf{y}=c\mathbf{1}$, i.e.\ $\mathbf{x}=c\mathbf{u}$.
nodes.statement_short: Equality iff x = c u.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Probability simplex Pi_n
nodes.statement: Denote by $\Pi_n\subset \mathbb{R}_+^n$ the set of probability vectors $\mathbf{p}=(p_1,\ldots,p_n)^\top$.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Donsker-Varadhan characterization for tensors
nodes.statement: Assume that $\mathcal{T}\in \mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$. Then \begin{equation} \log\rho(\mathcal{T})=\max_{(p_1,\ldots,p_n)^\top\in \Pi_n}\inf_{\mathbf{x}>\mathbf{0}}\sum_{i=1}^n p_i \log\frac{(\mathcal{T}\mathbf{x})_i}{x_i^{d-1}}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: log rho(T) is a max over probability vectors of an inf over positive x of averaged log Collatz-Wielandt ratios.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality
nodes.label: DVtens

nodes.name: Donsker-Varadhan formula (5.9)
nodes.statement: \log\rho(\mathcal{T})=\max_{(p_1,\ldots,p_n)^\top\in \Pi_n}\inf_{\mathbf{x}>\mathbf{0}}\sum_{i=1}^n p_i \log\frac{(\mathcal{T}\mathbf{x})_i}{x_i^{d-1}}.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality
nodes.label: DVten

nodes.name: Proof of the Donsker-Varadhan characterization
nodes.statement: Recall that Sion's theorem~\cite{sion} shows that \[\max_{p\in P}\inf_{y\in Y}L(p,y)=\inf_{y\in Y}\max_{p\in P}L(p,y) \] if $P$ is a convex compact subset of $\mathbb{R}^N$, $Y$ is a convex subset of $\mathbb{R}^M$, for all $\mathbf{y}\in Y$, $\mathbf{p}\mapsto L(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{y})$ is concave and upper semi-continuous, and for all $\mathbf{p}\in P$, $\mathbf{y}\mapsto L(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{y})$ is convex and lower semicontinuous. Let us apply this result to $P:=\Pi_n$, $B=\mathbb{R}^n$, \[ L(p,y) = \sum_{i=1}^n p_i \log((\mathcal{T}\exp(y))_i/\exp((d-1)y_i) \enspace . \] Here, the map $p\mapsto L(p,y)$ is linear, whereas the convexity of the map $y\mapsto L(p,y)$ follows from the fact that the set of log-convex functions is a convex cone~\cite{Kin61}. By the Collatz-Wielandt formula~\eqref{infmaxcharrho}, \begin{eqnarray} \log \rho(\mathcal{T})&= \inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}\max_{i\in[n]}\log((\mathcal{T}\exp(y))_i/\exp((d-1)y_i))\nonumber \\ &= \inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}\max_{p\in\Pi_n}\sum_{i\in [n]}p_i\log((\mathcal{T}\exp(y))_i/\exp((d-1)y_i)) \enspace. \nonumber \end{eqnarray} By Sion's theorem, we obtain~\eqref{DVten}.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Sion's minimax theorem to the Collatz-Wielandt formula written in log coordinates.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Recall Sion's minimax theorem
nodes.statement: Recall that Sion's theorem~\cite{sion} shows that \[\max_{p\in P}\inf_{y\in Y}L(p,y)=\inf_{y\in Y}\max_{p\in P}L(p,y) \] if $P$ is a convex compact subset of $\mathbb{R}^N$, $Y$ is a convex subset of $\mathbb{R}^M$, for all $\mathbf{y}\in Y$, $\mathbf{p}\mapsto L(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{y})$ is concave and upper semi-continuous, and for all $\mathbf{p}\in P$, $\mathbf{y}\mapsto L(\mathbf{p},\mathbf{y})$ is convex and lower semicontinuous.
nodes.statement_short: Recall Sion's minimax theorem.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Check Sion's hypotheses
nodes.statement: Let us apply this result to $P:=\Pi_n$, $B=\mathbb{R}^n$, \[ L(p,y) = \sum_{i=1}^n p_i \log((\mathcal{T}\exp(y))_i/\exp((d-1)y_i) \enspace . \] Here, the map $p\mapsto L(p,y)$ is linear, whereas the convexity of the map $y\mapsto L(p,y)$ follows from the fact that the set of log-convex functions is a convex cone~\cite{Kin61}.
nodes.statement_short: L is linear in p and convex in y by log-convexity.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Collatz-Wielandt in log form
nodes.statement: By the Collatz-Wielandt formula~\eqref{infmaxcharrho}, \begin{eqnarray} \log \rho(\mathcal{T})&= \inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}\max_{i\in[n]}\log((\mathcal{T}\exp(y))_i/\exp((d-1)y_i))\nonumber \\ &= \inf_{y\in\mathbb{R}^n}\max_{p\in\Pi_n}\sum_{i\in [n]}p_i\log((\mathcal{T}\exp(y))_i/\exp((d-1)y_i)) \enspace. \nonumber \end{eqnarray}
nodes.statement_short: Write log rho as inf-max over p in the simplex.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Swap inf and max
nodes.statement: By Sion's theorem, we obtain~\eqref{DVten}.
nodes.statement_short: Sion's theorem swaps inf and max, giving (5.9).
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 12 (omitted)
nodes.statement: The proof is identical to the proof in \cite{Fri81}, in which the theorem is deduced from the special case of Theorem~\ref{DVtens} concerning nonnegative matrices, so we omit it.
nodes.statement_short: Same as Fri81: deduce from the Donsker-Varadhan characterization (Theorem 11).
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Convex-function Donsker-Varadhan characterization
nodes.statement: Assume that $\mathcal{T}\in \mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$. Assume that $\Psi:\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}$ is a convex function. Suppose furthermore that $\Psi'(\log \rho(\mathcal{T}))\geqslant 0$. Then \[\Psi(\log\rho(\mathcal{T}))=\max_{(p_1,\ldots,p_n)^\top\in \Pi_n}\inf_{\mathbf{x}>\mathbf{0}}\sum_{i=1}^n p_i \Psi(\log\frac{(\mathcal{T}\mathbf{x})_i}{x_i^{d-1}}).\] In particular \begin{equation} \rho(\mathcal{T})=\max_{(p_1,\ldots,p_n)^\top\in \Pi_n}\inf_{\mathbf{x}>\mathbf{0}}\sum_{i=1}^n p_i \frac{(\mathcal{T}\mathbf{x})_i}{x_i^{d-1}}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The Donsker-Varadhan formula holds after composing with a convex Psi nondecreasing at log rho; in particular for rho itself.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality
assumptions: Assume that $\Psi:\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R}$ is a convex function.
nodes.label: thm3.3F

nodes.name: Donsker-Varadhan formula for rho (5.10)
nodes.statement: \rho(\mathcal{T})=\max_{(p_1,\ldots,p_n)^\top\in \Pi_n}\inf_{\mathbf{x}>\mathbf{0}}\sum_{i=1}^n p_i \frac{(\mathcal{T}\mathbf{x})_i}{x_i^{d-1}}.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality
nodes.label: DVten1

nodes.name: Convexity of the spectral radius in the diagonal entries
nodes.statement: The spectral radius of a tensor $\mathcal{T}=[t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]\in\mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$ is a convex function in the diagonal entries $(t_{1,\ldots,1},\ldots,t_{n,\ldots,n})^\top\in\mathbb{R}_+^n$.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality
conclusions: is a convex function in the diagonal entries $(t_{1,\ldots,1},\ldots,t_{n,\ldots,n})^\top\in\mathbb{R}_+^n$
nodes.label: convrhodiagel

nodes.name: Proof of convexity in the diagonal entries
nodes.statement: We showed that the spectral radius depends continuously on the entries of the tensor. Hence, arguing by density, we may assume that $\mathcal{T}$ is weakly irreducible. Let $\mathcal{T}'=[t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d'}]\in\mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$ where the diagonal entries of $\mathcal{T}'$ are zero, while nondiagonal entries are equal to the corresponding entries of $\mathcal{T}$. Then \[\inf_{\mathbf{x}>\mathbf{0} } \sum_{i=1}^n p_i\frac{\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x})_i}{x_i^{d-1}}=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i t_{i,\ldots,i} +\inf_{\mathbf{x}>\mathbf{0} } \sum_{i=1}^n p_i\frac{\mathcal{T}'(\mathbf{x})_i}{x_i^{d-1}}.\] Hence the supremum over $\Pi_n$ is a convex function in the diagonal entries.
nodes.statement_short: By density assume weak irreducibility; the Donsker-Varadhan inner inf is affine in the diagonal, so the sup is convex.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Reduce to weakly irreducible
nodes.statement: We showed that the spectral radius depends continuously on the entries of the tensor. Hence, arguing by density, we may assume that $\mathcal{T}$ is weakly irreducible.
nodes.statement_short: By continuity and density assume T weakly irreducible.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Split off the diagonal
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{T}'=[t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d'}]\in\mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$ where the diagonal entries of $\mathcal{T}'$ are zero, while nondiagonal entries are equal to the corresponding entries of $\mathcal{T}$. Then \[\inf_{\mathbf{x}>\mathbf{0} } \sum_{i=1}^n p_i\frac{\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{x})_i}{x_i^{d-1}}=\sum_{i=1}^n p_i t_{i,\ldots,i} +\inf_{\mathbf{x}>\mathbf{0} } \sum_{i=1}^n p_i\frac{\mathcal{T}'(\mathbf{x})_i}{x_i^{d-1}}.\]
nodes.statement_short: The inner infimum is affine in the diagonal entries.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Supremum of affine functions
nodes.statement: Hence the supremum over $\Pi_n$ is a convex function in the diagonal entries.
nodes.statement_short: A supremum of affine functions is convex.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Friedland-Karlin diagonal scaling theorem for matrices
nodes.statement: Suppose that $A\in\mathbb{R}_+^{n\times n}$ is irreducible and all diagonal entries are positive. Let $\mathbf{u},\mathbf{w}$ two positive vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then there exists a matrix $B$ diagonally equivalent to $A$, i.e.\ $B=\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(e^{\mathbf{y}})A\mathop{{\rm diag}}\nolimits(e^{\mathbf{z}})$ such that $B\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u}, B^\top \mathbf{w}=\mathbf{w}$.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality
assumptions: Suppose that $A\in\mathbb{R}_+^{n\times n}$ is irreducible and all diagonal entries are positive.
conclusions: there exists a matrix $B$ diagonally equivalent to $A$

nodes.name: Diagonally equivalent tensors
nodes.statement: We say that tensors $\mathcal{T}=[t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}],\mathcal{T}'=[t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}'],\in \mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$ are diagonally equivalent if $t'_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}=t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}e^{b_{i_1}+\sum_{j=2}^d c_{i_j}}$ for all $i_1,\ldots,i_d\in [n]$ for some $\mathbf{b}=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)^\top, \mathbf{c}=(c_1,\ldots,c_n)^\top\in\mathbb{R}^n$.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Diagonal scaling of tensors to prescribed Perron vectors
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{T}'\in \mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$ be an irreducible tensor with positive diagonal entries. Let $\mathbf{u},\mathbf{w}$ be two given positive vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfying $\sum_{i=1}^n u_iw_i=1$. Then there exists a diagonal equivalent tensor $\mathcal{T}$ to $\mathcal{T}'$ which satisfies the following conditions. First, $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{u}^{\circ (d-1)}$. Second \eqref{defpropA} holds with $\rho(\mathcal{T})=1$.
nodes.statement_short: An irreducible tensor with positive diagonal can be diagonally rescaled so that given u, w are its right and left Perron vectors with rho=1.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality
assumptions: Let $\mathcal{T}'\in \mathbb{R}_{ps,+}^{n^{\times d}}$ be an irreducible tensor with positive diagonal entries.
Let $\mathbf{u},\mathbf{w}$ be two given positive vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ satisfying $\sum_{i=1}^n u_iw_i=1$.
conclusions: there exists a diagonal equivalent tensor $\mathcal{T}$ to $\mathcal{T}'$ which satisfies the following conditions
nodes.label: diagteneqthm

nodes.name: Proof of the diagonal scaling theorem
nodes.statement: Consider the convex function $f(\mathbf{x},\mathcal{T}'):=\sum_{i=1}^n u_iw_i (\log\mathcal{T}'(e^{\mathbf{x}})_i -(d-1)x_i)$ on the hyperplane $H=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n,\sum_{i=1} x_i=0\}$. Observe that since the diagonal entries of $\mathcal{T}$ are positive we obtain that each expression $\mathcal{T}'(e^{\mathbf{x}})_i e^{-(d-1)x_i}\geqslant t_{i,\ldots,i}$. That is $ u_iw_i (\log\mathcal{T}'(e^{\mathbf{x}})_i -(d-1)x_i)\geqslant u_iw_i \log t_{i,\ldots,i}$ for each $i\in [n]$. We claim, as in \cite{FK75}, that $\lim _{k\to\infty}f(\mathbf{x}_k,\mathcal{T}')=\infty$ for any sequence $\mathbf{x}_k=(x_{1,k},\ldots,x_{n,k})^\top\in H$ such that $\lim_{k\to\infty} \|\mathbf{x}_{k}\|=\infty$. Indeed by taking a subsequence and renaming the coordinates $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ we can assume the following conditions. First $x_{1,k}\leqslant \ldots\leqslant x_{n,k}$ for each positive integer $k$. Furthermore, there there exists $l\in [n-1]$ such that $\lim_{k\to\infty}x_{i,k}=-\infty$ for $i\in[l]$, and $x_{l+1,k}\geqslant a (\in\mathbb{R})$ for each positive integer $k$. Since $\mathcal{T}'$ is irreducible there $i\in[l-1]$ and $j_1,\ldots,j_{d-1}\in[n]\setminus [l-1]$ such that $t_{i,j_1,\ldots,,j_{d-1}}>0$. Hence $\mathcal{T}'(e^{\mathbf{x}_k})_i e^{-(d-1)x_{i,k}}\geqslant t_{i,j_1,\ldots,j_{d-1}}e^{(d-1)(a-x_{i,k})}$. Thus $\lim_{k\to \infty}\mathcal{T}'(e^{\mathbf{x}_k})_i e^{-(d-1)x_{i,k}}=\infty$, which implies that $\lim _{k\to\infty}f(\mathbf{x}_k,\mathcal{T}')=\infty$. Hence $f(\mathbf{x},\mathcal{T}')$ achieves its minimum at some critical point $\mathbf{y}\in H$. Let $\mathbf{1}=(1,\ldots,1)^\top$. Observe that $f(\mathbf{x},\mathcal{T}')=f(\mathbf{x}+t\mathbf{1})$ for any $t\in\mathbb{R}$. Thus the minimum of $f(\mathbf{x},\mathcal{T}')$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is achieved at each point of the form $\mathbf{y}+t\mathbf{1}$. We now study the effects of rescaling of $\mathcal{T}'$. First, consider the rescaling $\tilde{\mathcal{T}}=[\tilde t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]$, where $\tilde t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}=e^{a_{i_1}} t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}$ for some $\mathbf{a}=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)^\top\in\mathbb{R}^n$. Then the minimum of $f(\mathbf{x},\tilde{\mathcal{T}})$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is achieved at $\mathbf{y}+t\mathbf{1}$. Second, consider the rescaling $\hat{\mathcal{T}}=[\hat t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]$, where $\hat t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}=e^{\sum_{j=2}^d b_{i_j}} t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}$ for some $\mathbf{b}=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)^\top\in\mathbb{R}^n$. Then the minimum of $f(\mathbf{x},\hat{\mathcal{T}})$ is achieved at the points $\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{1}$. Now choose $\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{y}-\log\mathbf{u}$. Then the minimum of $f(\mathbf{x},\hat{\mathcal{T}})$ is achieved at the point $\log\mathbf{u}$. Finally, rescale $\hat{\mathcal{T}}$ to obtain $\mathcal{T}=[t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]$, where $t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}=e^{a_{i_1}} t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}$ for a unique $\mathbf{a}=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)^\top\in\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{u}^{\circ (d-1)}$. In particular $\rho(\mathcal{T})=1$ and \eqref{pratTuid} holds. Therefore the first equality of \eqref{defpropA} holds. As $\log\mathbf{u}$ is a minimal point of $f(\mathbf{x},\mathcal{T})$ we deduce by straightforward calculations that the second equality of \eqref{defpropA} holds.
nodes.statement_short: Minimize a coercive convex function on a hyperplane and rescale. Key step: coercivity via irreducibility, as in FK75.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Convex objective and lower bound
nodes.statement: Consider the convex function $f(\mathbf{x},\mathcal{T}'):=\sum_{i=1}^n u_iw_i (\log\mathcal{T}'(e^{\mathbf{x}})_i -(d-1)x_i)$ on the hyperplane $H=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^n,\sum_{i=1} x_i=0\}$. Observe that since the diagonal entries of $\mathcal{T}$ are positive we obtain that each expression $\mathcal{T}'(e^{\mathbf{x}})_i e^{-(d-1)x_i}\geqslant t_{i,\ldots,i}$. That is $ u_iw_i (\log\mathcal{T}'(e^{\mathbf{x}})_i -(d-1)x_i)\geqslant u_iw_i \log t_{i,\ldots,i}$ for each $i\in [n]$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the convex function f(x, T') on the hyperplane H; positive diagonal bounds each term from below.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Coercivity of f
nodes.statement: We claim, as in \cite{FK75}, that $\lim _{k\to\infty}f(\mathbf{x}_k,\mathcal{T}')=\infty$ for any sequence $\mathbf{x}_k=(x_{1,k},\ldots,x_{n,k})^\top\in H$ such that $\lim_{k\to\infty} \|\mathbf{x}_{k}\|=\infty$. Indeed by taking a subsequence and renaming the coordinates $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ we can assume the following conditions. First $x_{1,k}\leqslant \ldots\leqslant x_{n,k}$ for each positive integer $k$. Furthermore, there there exists $l\in [n-1]$ such that $\lim_{k\to\infty}x_{i,k}=-\infty$ for $i\in[l]$, and $x_{l+1,k}\geqslant a (\in\mathbb{R})$ for each positive integer $k$. Since $\mathcal{T}'$ is irreducible there $i\in[l-1]$ and $j_1,\ldots,j_{d-1}\in[n]\setminus [l-1]$ such that $t_{i,j_1,\ldots,,j_{d-1}}>0$. Hence $\mathcal{T}'(e^{\mathbf{x}_k})_i e^{-(d-1)x_{i,k}}\geqslant t_{i,j_1,\ldots,j_{d-1}}e^{(d-1)(a-x_{i,k})}$. Thus $\lim_{k\to \infty}\mathcal{T}'(e^{\mathbf{x}_k})_i e^{-(d-1)x_{i,k}}=\infty$, which implies that $\lim _{k\to\infty}f(\mathbf{x}_k,\mathcal{T}')=\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: f tends to infinity along unbounded sequences in H.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Normalize the diverging sequence
nodes.statement: Indeed by taking a subsequence and renaming the coordinates $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ we can assume the following conditions. First $x_{1,k}\leqslant \ldots\leqslant x_{n,k}$ for each positive integer $k$. Furthermore, there there exists $l\in [n-1]$ such that $\lim_{k\to\infty}x_{i,k}=-\infty$ for $i\in[l]$, and $x_{l+1,k}\geqslant a (\in\mathbb{R})$ for each positive integer $k$.
nodes.statement_short: Pass to a subsequence with sorted coordinates, some going to -infinity.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Irreducibility forces blow-up
nodes.statement: Since $\mathcal{T}'$ is irreducible there $i\in[l-1]$ and $j_1,\ldots,j_{d-1}\in[n]\setminus [l-1]$ such that $t_{i,j_1,\ldots,,j_{d-1}}>0$. Hence $\mathcal{T}'(e^{\mathbf{x}_k})_i e^{-(d-1)x_{i,k}}\geqslant t_{i,j_1,\ldots,j_{d-1}}e^{(d-1)(a-x_{i,k})}$. Thus $\lim_{k\to \infty}\mathcal{T}'(e^{\mathbf{x}_k})_i e^{-(d-1)x_{i,k}}=\infty$, which implies that $\lim _{k\to\infty}f(\mathbf{x}_k,\mathcal{T}')=\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Irreducibility gives a positive entry forcing f to infinity.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Existence of a minimizer
nodes.statement: Hence $f(\mathbf{x},\mathcal{T}')$ achieves its minimum at some critical point $\mathbf{y}\in H$. Let $\mathbf{1}=(1,\ldots,1)^\top$. Observe that $f(\mathbf{x},\mathcal{T}')=f(\mathbf{x}+t\mathbf{1})$ for any $t\in\mathbb{R}$. Thus the minimum of $f(\mathbf{x},\mathcal{T}')$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is achieved at each point of the form $\mathbf{y}+t\mathbf{1}$.
nodes.statement_short: f attains its minimum along a line y + t1.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Effect of rescalings
nodes.statement: We now study the effects of rescaling of $\mathcal{T}'$. First, consider the rescaling $\tilde{\mathcal{T}}=[\tilde t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]$, where $\tilde t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}=e^{a_{i_1}} t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}$ for some $\mathbf{a}=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)^\top\in\mathbb{R}^n$. Then the minimum of $f(\mathbf{x},\tilde{\mathcal{T}})$ on $\mathbb{R}^n$ is achieved at $\mathbf{y}+t\mathbf{1}$. Second, consider the rescaling $\hat{\mathcal{T}}=[\hat t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]$, where $\hat t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}=e^{\sum_{j=2}^d b_{i_j}} t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}$ for some $\mathbf{b}=(b_1,\ldots,b_n)^\top\in\mathbb{R}^n$. Then the minimum of $f(\mathbf{x},\hat{\mathcal{T}})$ is achieved at the points $\mathbf{y}-\mathbf{b}+t\mathbf{1}$. Now choose $\mathbf{b}=\mathbf{y}-\log\mathbf{u}$. Then the minimum of $f(\mathbf{x},\hat{\mathcal{T}})$ is achieved at the point $\log\mathbf{u}$.
nodes.statement_short: Row and column rescalings shift the minimizer; choose b so the minimum is at log u.
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Final row rescaling
nodes.statement: Finally, rescale $\hat{\mathcal{T}}$ to obtain $\mathcal{T}=[t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}]$, where $t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}=e^{a_{i_1}} t_{i_1,\ldots,i_d}$ for a unique $\mathbf{a}=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)^\top\in\mathbb{R}^n$ such that $\mathcal{T}(\mathbf{u})=\mathbf{u}^{\circ (d-1)}$. In particular $\rho(\mathcal{T})=1$ and \eqref{pratTuid} holds. Therefore the first equality of \eqref{defpropA} holds. As $\log\mathbf{u}$ is a minimal point of $f(\mathbf{x},\mathcal{T})$ we deduce by straightforward calculations that the second equality of \eqref{defpropA} holds.
nodes.statement_short: A last row scaling gives T(u) = u^{[d-1]}, rho = 1, and both identities of (3.18).
nodes.section: 5 Generalization of Friedland-Karlin inequality

nodes.name: Occupation measure (matrix)
nodes.statement: A nonnegative matrix $\mu=[\mu_{ij}]\in \mathbb{R}_+^{n \times n}$ is called an {\em occupation measure} if the following conditions are satisfied: \begin{equation} \sum_{i,j=1}^n \mu_{ij}=1, \quad \sum_{j=1}^n \mu_{ij}=\sum_{j=1}^n\mu_{ji}, \textrm{ for all }i\in[n], \;\mu\in \mathbb{R}_+^{n \times n}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 6.1 Entropic characterization of the spectral radius of a nonnegative matrix

nodes.name: Occupation measure conditions (6.1)
nodes.statement: \sum_{i,j=1}^n \mu_{ij}=1, \quad \sum_{j=1}^n \mu_{ij}=\sum_{j=1}^n\mu_{ji}, \textrm{ for all }i\in[n], \;\mu\in \mathbb{R}_+^{n \times n}.
nodes.section: 6.1 Entropic characterization of the spectral radius of a nonnegative matrix
nodes.label: defmatocme

nodes.name: Flow interpretation of occupation measures
nodes.statement: There is a natural interpretation of an occupation measure in terms of weights on the directed graph $\vec{K}_n$ on the set of vertices $[n]$. Assume that the weight of each diedge $(i,j)$, the edge from $i$ to $j$ is the $\mu_{ij}$. The first condition of \eqref{defmatocme} means that $\mu$ is a probability measure on the $n^2$ diedges of $\vec{K}_n$. The second condition of \eqref{defmatocme} can be easily explained in terms of flow (circulation), whose value on the diedge $(i,j)$ is $\mu_{ij}$. Namely, for each vertex $i$ the sum of the flow out of the vertex $i$ is equal to the sum of the flow into the vertex $i$.
nodes.statement_short: An occupation measure is a probability circulation on the arcs of the complete digraph K_n.
nodes.section: 6.1 Entropic characterization of the spectral radius of a nonnegative matrix

nodes.name: Dicycle
nodes.statement: A sequence $\gamma$ of diedges is called a {\em dicycle of length} $k$ in $\vec{K}_n$, if there exists $k$ distinct vertices $i_1,\ldots,i_k\in [n]$ such that the $k$ diedges of $\gamma$ are $(i_1,i_2)$, \ldots, $(i_{k-1},i_k),(i_k,i_1)$. A dicycle of length one is the edge $(i_1,i_1)$.
nodes.section: 6.1 Entropic characterization of the spectral radius of a nonnegative matrix

nodes.name: Set of dicycles Sigma_n
nodes.statement: Denote by $\Sigma_n$ the collections of all dicycles in $\vec{K}_n$.
nodes.section: 6.1 Entropic characterization of the spectral radius of a nonnegative matrix

nodes.name: Cycle occupation measure mu(gamma)
nodes.statement: To each cycle $\gamma$ we associate the following occupation measure $\mu(\gamma)$. Assume that the length of the cycle is $k$. then the weight of each edge in the cycle $\gamma$ is $\frac{1}{k}$. Other edges have weight zero.
nodes.section: 6.1 Entropic characterization of the spectral radius of a nonnegative matrix

nodes.name: Set of occupation measures Omega(n)
nodes.statement: Denote by $\Omega(n)\subset\mathbb{R}_+^{n \times n}$ the compact convex set of occupation measure.
nodes.section: 6.1 Entropic characterization of the spectral radius of a nonnegative matrix

nodes.name: Occupation measures supported in S
nodes.statement: For a subset $S\subseteq [n]\times [n]$ denote by $\Omega(n, S)\subseteq \Omega(n)$ the subset of all occupation measures whose support is contained in $S$.
nodes.section: 6.1 Entropic characterization of the spectral radius of a nonnegative matrix

nodes.name: Extreme points of the occupation measure polytope
nodes.statement: The extreme points of $\Omega(n)$ are the occupation measures $\mu(\gamma)$, where $\gamma\in \Sigma_n$. Let $S\subset [n]\times [n]$. Then $\Omega(n, S)\ne \emptyset$ if and only if $S$ contains a dicycle. Suppose that $S$ contains a dicycle. Then $\Omega(n, S)$ is a nonempty compact convex set, whose extreme point are $\mu(\gamma)$, where $\gamma$ are all dicycles in $S$.
nodes.statement_short: Extreme points of Omega(n) (and of Omega(n,S)) are the uniform cycle measures mu(gamma).
nodes.section: 6.1 Entropic characterization of the spectral radius of a nonnegative matrix
conclusions: The extreme points of $\Omega(n)$ are the occupation measures $\mu(\gamma)$, where $\gamma\in \Sigma_n$.
$\Omega(n, S)\ne \emptyset$ if and only if $S$ contains a dicycle
nodes.label: extptdOmega

nodes.name: Proof of the extreme point lemma
nodes.statement: We first prove that if $\mu\in \Omega(n)$ then the support of $\mu$ contains a dicycle $\gamma$. Assume to the contrary that it is not the case. Since $\mu$ is a probability measure on $\vec{K}_n$ it follows that there exists $\mu_{i_1i_2}>0$. As the support of $\mu$ does not contain a dicycle we have that $i_1\ne i_2$. The first condition of \eqref{defmatocme} for $i=i_2$ implies that there exists $i_3$ such that $\mu_{i_2i_3}>0$. Since the support of does not contain a cycle we get that $i_3\notin \{i_1,i_2\}$. Continuing in this manner we deduce \ that in the step $k$ we have $k+1$ distinct in indices $i_1,\ldots,i_{k+1}$ such that $\mu_{i_pi_{p+1}}>0$ for $p\in[k]$. For $k=n$ we obtain the contradiction. We now show that the convex set spanned by the set $E(n)=\{\mu(\gamma), \gamma\in\Sigma_n\}$ is $\Omega(n)$. For $p\in[n^2]$ denote by $\Omega_p(n)$ the subset of all occupation measures with at most $p\geqslant 1$ nonzero entries. We show by induction that the convex set spanned by $E(n)$ contains $\Omega_p(n)$. For $p=1$ the set $\Omega_p(n)$ consists of all $\mu(\gamma)$, where $\gamma$ is a dicycle of length one. Suppose that the claim holds for $p\leqslant q$. Assume that $p=q+1$. Let $\mu\in \Omega(n)$ has exactly $q+1$ nonzero entry. Assume a dicycle $\gamma$ in the support of $\mu$. If $\mu=\mu(\gamma)$ we are done. Otherwise, let $a>0$ be the maximal $b>0$ such that $\mu -b\mu(\gamma)\geqslant 0$. Then $\mu_1:=\frac{1}{1-a}(\mu-\mu(\gamma))\in \Omega_{q}(n)$. So $\mu_1$ is a convex combination of measures in $E(n)$. As $\mu=(1-a)\mu_1+a\mu(\gamma)$ it follows that $\mu$ is a convex combination of some $\mu(\gamma)$. Hence the set of the extreme points of $\Omega(n)$ is contained in $E(n)$. Clearly, $\mu(\gamma)$ is not a convex combination of the measures in $E(n)\setminus\{\mu(\gamma)\}$. Hence $E(n)$ is the set of the extreme points of $\Omega(n)$. The other claims of the lemma follow straightforwardly from the above arguments.
nodes.statement_short: Supports contain dicycles (else an infinite simple path); peel off cycle measures by induction on support size.

nodes.name: Occupation measures and stochastic matrices
nodes.statement: Denote by $\operatorname{Stoc}(n)\subset \mathbb{R}_+^{n\times n}$ the convex set of (row) stochastic matrices. Then there exists a map $\Psi_n: \Omega(n)\to \operatorname{Stoc}(n)$ and a multivalued map $\Phi_n: \operatorname{Stoc}(n)\to\Omega(n)$ with the following properties. \begin{enumerate} \item For each $A\in \operatorname{Stoc}(n)$ the set $\Phi_n(A)$ is a closed nonempty convex set of occupation measures. \item $\Phi_n(A)$ consists of a unique occupation measure if and only if $1$ is a simple root of $\det(zI-A)$. \item If $A\in \operatorname{Stoc}(n)$ is irreducible then $\Phi_n(A)$ consists of a unique occupation measure $\mu(A)$ which is irreducible. Furthermore, $\Psi_n(\mu(A))=A$. \item If $\mu\in\Omega(n)$ is irreducible then $\Psi_n(\mu)$ is irreducible and $\Phi_n(\Psi_n(\mu))=\{\mu\}$. \item For each $\mu\in\Omega(n)$ the convex set $\Phi_n(\Psi_n(\mu))$ contains $\mu$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Maps between occupation measures and stochastic matrices (via stationary distributions), bijective on irreducible ones.
nodes.section: 6.1 Entropic characterization of the spectral radius of a nonnegative matrix
conclusions: there exists a map $\Psi_n: \Omega(n)\to \operatorname{Stoc}(n)$ and a multivalued map $\Phi_n: \operatorname{Stoc}(n)\to\Omega(n)$ with the following properties
